If the flight crew gives no command during decompression, the cabin crew contacts the flight crew by interphone as soon as possible and makes sure that they have put on their oxygen masks. If it is not possible to contact the flight crew, the nearest Cabin Crew Member enters the cockpit, with the nearest portable oxygen cylinder, by opening the cockpit door directly if it has been unlocked automatically, or by using the cockpit door emergency password (depending on the aircraft type) if the door is not unlocked. S/he confirms that the flight crew members are using their oxygen masks and capable of communicating. If s/he notices that the flight crew members are unable to inhale oxygen, s/he provides the flight crew with oxygen by using the cockpit oxygen system in compliance with the methods defined in EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual, Section 8.3.6 Incapacitated Pilot paragraph (b). The conscious flight crew members are given priority.  8.3.2.2.1. Manual Opening of Oxygen Mask Covers  The oxygen mask covers in the passenger service unit and the mask covers in the lavatory, galley, crew rest, and cabin crew stations are opened manually by using the pin or hook of MRT (or by using the PSU Latch Button on board B787 aircraft). The detailed information on the subject is available in the requirements in   EK.10.71.003 Cabin Crew Aircraft Types Manual.  8.3.2.3. Cockpit Oxygen System  The cockpit oxygen system is a system with gas. The use of cockpit oxygen mask is explained in EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual, Section 8.3.6 Incapacitated Pilot.  8.3.3. Fire  Fire, originating inside the cabin, may quickly spread due to the interior air conditioning system, and may get out of control within 30 seconds. Duty of the cabin crew is to prevent the occurrence of a fire on board. 3 factors generating a fire are heat, oxygen and flammable materials. When these factors come together through a chemical reaction, the fire breaks out. At least one of the factors leading to the fire shall be eliminated in order to extinguish the fire. The method to be followed is listed below: Isolating from oxygen (by covering with such materials as blanket, coat, topcoat, etc.), Cooling (by using a water-based liquid such as coffee, tea, water, etc.), Disposing the flammable material. In case of fire, flow of information shall be ensured to the flight crew at all stages such as place and progress of fire, method and result of intervention. Procedures to be applied by the Cabin Crew Members in case of a fire are described in detail in the   Quick Reference Handlist (QRH), Section 1.23. Fire Fighting.  8.3.3.1. Categorization of Fire  1- Type A (Simple) Fire and Extinguishers  Type A fires are the ones generated due to flammable and simple materials (paper, fabric, wood, etc.). Fire shall be extinguished by cooling method. Thereby, temperature of the burning material will be ensured to decrease below its flash point. During a type A fire, water glycol extinguisher shall be used, if available. In case of simple fires, the optimum method is to isolate the burning object from oxygen by covering it with a blanket. In addition to water glycol extinguisher, BCF or 2-BTP type extinguisher may also be used in Type A fire.  2- Type B (Chemical) Fire and Extinguishers  Type B fires are the ones generated due to any flammable liquid and chemical substances. The most effective way of extinguishing is isolating it from oxygen. BCF or 2-BTP type fire extinguishers shall be used. Since the chemical substances are lighter than water, and they will diffuse in the water causing the fire to get stronger; the water-based or water glycol extinguishers shall not be used for such type of fires.  3- Type C (Electrical) Fire and Extinguishers  Type C fires are the ones generated by electrically powered tools or electric cables. The most appropriate method for extinguishing this type of fires is to use BCF or 2-BTP type fire extinguishers. Before starting to extinguish, all circuit breakers shall be turned OFF. The cables shall be cut off by use of an axe, upon the approval by the Commander, if necessary. === Sayfa 171 ===
Since the liquids generate electricity, water glycol extinguishers or any other liquid shall not be used for such fires.  8.3.3.2. Types of Fire 8.3.3.2.1. Fire in Cabin  The materials carried in the cabin by the passengers may cause fire; therefore, the cabin crew must observe the cabin continuously against any possible fire. UV lighters may give rise to a high flame due to any leakage or pressurization in the cabin. Batteries carried in pocket may give rise to a fire due to short circuit.  1- Fabric Fires  Cover it by use of a blanket or coat. Pour water or nonflammable liquid on it. Use water glycol extinguisher, if available.  2- Fire in Overhead Bin  In the event that the electrical devices, placed inside the overhead bins, are noticed by the cabin crew members; it shall be confirmed with the concerned passenger that they are at “OFF” position. Wear smoke hood and Kevlar gloves. Open the overhead bin lid slightly. Discharge the BCF or 2-BTP by raking the inside of the overhead bin. Close the overhead bin and wait for 30 seconds. Use BCF or 2-BTP once more. Observe the section, where the fire occurred. Take all the items inside the overhead bin out, and cool them by use of a non-flammable liquid.  3- Seat Fire  Keep in mind that the fire may have arisen from an electrical origin, PED Power or handset. Turn off the IFE system immediately. The flight crew shall be informed, and the IFE system shall be disconnected from the circuit breaker by the flight crew. Wear smoke hood and kevlar gloves. Make a hole on the panel that includes the electrical system of the seat by using the axe, if necessary. Use BCF or 2-BTP. Observe the section, where the fire occurred.  4- Blanket and Carpet Fire  Cover it by use of another blanket or coat, jacket etc. Use water glycol extinguisher, if available.  5- Fire on a Person's Clothes  Cover the person by use of a blanket, coat or jacket by laying her/him down on the aisle. Press the blanket, etc. down by hand in order to isolate the burning part of the person from oxygen. Remove the blanket, coat or jacket, etc. slowly and carefully, after the fire is definitely extinguished. === Sayfa 172 ===
Do not apply any kind of fire extinguisher or nonflammable liquid (water, fruit juice) on the person.  6- Fire in the Cabin Side-Panel  In case of a fire from the electric cable between the cabin panels, the smoke will spread from panels and air conditioning system of the aircraft to the cabin. In that case; Wear smoke hood and protective gloves. Slightly lift the edge of the panel by the hook of the axe. Discharge the BCF or 2-BTP from this gap, then; close the panel and wait for 30 seconds. Repeat such action, until the fire is definitely extinguished. Keep the section under surveillance.  Note:   If the panel cannot be opened slightly from the edges; make a small hole by use of an axe, and discharge the BCF or 2-BTP through this hole.  7- Lithium Battery Fire  Lithium batteries are used in devices such as mobile phones, electronic books, smart luggage, cameras, MP3 players, computers, tablets, etc. The measures to be taken for the lithium battery fires are available in the requirements specified in   EK.10.73.001 Operation Manual Part-A, Section 8.3.15.1.6 Safety Precautions on Use of Flight Crew Member’s PEDs. Electronic devices containing lithium batteries may cause the sudden explosion of battery cells and fire due to overheating or damage caused by crushing. Against such kind of fires, if the cabin crew members detect any devices such as computers, etc. placed in the overhead bins in operating state, they ensure that the device is switched off and placed in the overhead bins in non-operating state in all phases of the flight. All electronic devices connected to electrical power unit shall be kept under surveillance during the flight and disconnected from the electrical power unit during take-off and landing. In the event that an electronic device falls between the electrically-controlled seats; the seat shall not be moved electrically and mechanically and the seat of the passenger is changed, if possible, the flight crew is informed of the situation, and if the seat is to be moved, measures are taken against the risk of fire due to the compression and smashing of lithium battery. In the event that personal electronic devices are charged on board, they shall be observed and monitored by the cabin crew members to prevent the risk of short circuit due to overcharging. In the case of suspicion of fire due to overcharging/short circuit, PED power is switched OFF to cut the power of all seat sockets. It is dangerous to use spare batteries/power banks on board. Spare batteries/power banks are not permitted to be charged and used on board. In case of lithium battery fire; Upon noticing a failed device, it is important to take action immediately, especially before it catches on fire. If there is no injury risk, the first thing to do must be to switch off the device, unplug it, or disconnect the device from power. Wear smoke hood and protective gloves. Use BCF or 2-BTP. Place the electronic device in a metal box (waste bin in lavatory etc. may be used by removing the garbage bag). Pour water to exceed the device. Do not use ice for cooling. Keep the metal box under surveillance throughout the flight in an area separate from all emergency equipment. If the fire is in the cockpit, the Commander decides on the safest action plan between removing the device from the cockpit and leaving it in the cockpit. Do not attempt to take or move any device fuming or burning from within unless you have taken the necessary fire protection measures. If it is not possible to hold the device, you can use axe to remove it from the cockpit properly (by pushing and pulling). Immediately after extinguishing the fire and removing the device from the cockpit, one crew member puts the device in a metal box and pours water, water extinguisher, water-based non-flammable liquid on it to cool the battery and prevent the other battery cells from exposure to thermal runaway. The following points must be specified while reporting a lithium battery fire through AQD: What is the brand and model of the electronic device causing fire? Is it the original battery of the product? Was the device being charged as the fire started? Did the charging cable belong to the passenger who is the owner of the device? Was it provided by the cabin crew?  8.3.3.2.2. Fire in Lavatories  1- Places Where Lavatory Fires May Occur;  Heaters, Flush engine, Waste bins, Cables behind the lavatory walls. There is a built-in fire extinguisher under the washbasin of each lavatory, and smoke detectors on the ceilings, generating a warning when smoke is detected. These fire extinguishers contain a system, detecting the fire originating from the heaters or the waste bins, and extinguishing the same automatically. In order that system can be activated, the lid of the waste bin under the lavatory and the spring-loaded upper cover are required to be closed completely. If any defect that prevents these covers from being closed fully is detected, the flight crew is informed of the situation. The principles of checking the fixed fire extinguishers during the ground checks before the flight are available in   EK.10.71.003 Cabin Crew Aircraft Types Manual.  2- Preliminary Warnings During Lavatory Fires;  Smoke, arising from a fire, prompts the smoke detector to generate a warning. In case of any failure of the electrical devices inside the lavatory, circuit breaker of such devices in the cockpit will be tripped. The pins controlling the tap will warm up during the fires, originating from the heaters underneath the washbasins. Vapor will come out of the taps instead of water, and the washbasin will reach a temperature making it impossible to touch. In case of a fire in the flush engines, external surface of the engine casing will warm up. In case of a fire originating from the cables between the lavatory walls, the external walls will warm up. If the smoke detector is activated by a smoking passenger; check whether the cigarette butt has been thrown inside the waste bin after putting it out first.  Actions required to be taken by cabin crew members: If the lavatory door is hot and smoke is releasing through door apertures;  1- Keep the lavatory door closed. 2- Check the heat of the lavatory door with the back of your hand. 3- Make ready the equipment to be used during firefighting (extinguisher, smoke hood, axe, flashlight, protective gloves). 4- Put on the smoke hood when all the equipment is readily available. Stay behind the door, and open it carefully. Stay below the smoke level to protect yourself from the smoke and to ensure vision. 5- Identify the source of the fire by use of flashlight, if there is no flame. 6- If flames are visible, spray the extinguisher towards the source of the fire. 7- Close the door after making sure that the fire has completely been extinguished. 8- If the fire is in the waste bin, open the cover and discharge the extinguisher to such waste bin (water glycol extinguisher may be used). 9- If it is an electrical fire, it may arise from the electric panel inside the lavatory, heaters underneath the washbasins, flush engine or cables behind the lavatory walls. In such case, open a small hole on the panel or wall with an axe, and apply the fire extinguisher. 10- Frequently check the lavatory against a potential re-occurrence of fire, remove the waste bin and inflammable materials (such as Kleenex, seat cover, etc.) from the lavatory; and wet them with a liquid, if required, and close the lavatory for use. Do not place materials/substances out-of-purpose inside the oven (breadbasket, paper tissue, etc.). Check to make sure that there is no material out-of-purpose left inside the oven, before and after use. Make sure that no foreign object is attached on the food containers loaded by catering. In the event that   “No water”   warning is visible on the oven display, do not use the steam option, and record it in the e-CML/p-CML.  In Case of a Fire in Electric Panels;  1. Turn OFF the switches and circuit breakers. 2. Use BCF or 2-BTP. If   “Over heat, No water, Low water”   warning is visible, do not use the electric system, or water of the relevant system in the panels originating the warning; and record the incident in the e-CML/p-CML. During the flight operation: The tags and “inop/do not use” stickers attached to the fuses are not removed. Firefighting  A. Points to consider in case of Fire:  1. Identify the type and category of the fire. 2. Use the fire extinguisher appropriate for the fire type. 3. Be aware of the expiry date of the extinguisher. 4. Be familiar with the effect of the extinguisher's content on people, environment and fire. 5. Make sure that another Cabin Crew Member is readily waiting with a fire extinguisher, and always use the same type of extinguisher cylinders. Source of the fire may not be identified due to smoke. The most important point is to apply the fire extinguisher to the source of the fire. If the extinguisher is discharged towards the smoke or flames, fire may not be extinguished. In all cases, approach to the fire only as much as possible (1.5-2 m). Discharge the extinguisher to the source of the fire. Use the fire extinguisher, until the fire is completely extinguished. Keep a second extinguisher ready for use, if a fire extinguisher is not sufficient. Another cabin crew member shall immediately inform the flight crew and the cabin chief about the fire category, type, location, area where it has spread, method of intervention by cabin crew members, whether any change in passenger seats has been made, and if the passengers are under control or not (panic and chaos), and shall establish the required communication during firefighting process. In case of fire and/or smoke, cockpit door shall not be opened, and the flight crew members shall be informed through interphone. Cabin crew members shall not excite the passengers. Passengers shall be moved away from the area where such fire or smoke has occurred. Cabin crew members combating the fire shall protect themselves against toxic gas and smoke by means of PBE/Smoke Hood. If there is a trolley in the cabin, the trolley is secured in the galley, if possible, by the Cabin Crew Members who are not fighting the fire, so as not to prevent firefighting. If the trolley cannot be pulled into the galley, it is secured by crossing it in the cabin and pressing the brake pedal. If it is observed that passengers are in panic, flight crew shall be immediately informed and requested to make a calming announcement.  Flammable Materials  If you notice bottles or containers which contain highly inflammable or volatile liquids inside the cabin, immediately inform the flight crew about the matter.  B. Formation of Smoke  1. Smoke inside the cabin is not a normal situation. 2. The most major problem is to fail in identifying the source of the smoke. 3. Smoke may be observed at a point far from the source of the fire. 4. Smoke and heat will rise towards the ceiling of the cabin. 5. Density of the smoke is not always in proportion to the size of the fire. 6. Smoke may be toxic.  C. Protection From Smoke  Any object on fire emits dense smoke or toxic gases. Fire can be quickly taken under control, under many circumstances. Passengers closest to the source of smoke or fire shall be seated elsewhere for their safety and comfort. If panic appears to be spreading among the passengers, inform the flight crew immediately. If a dense smoke covers the cabin, cabin crews shall take the following actions through the “1.22. Smoke Announcement” specified in the   Quick Reference Handlist (QRH): 1. The cabin oxygen system is used in case of decompression. They cannot be used against smoke.  8.3.3.5.1. Built-in Fire Extinguishing System  Information on the control and operating principles of fixed fire extinguishing systems varying according to aircraft type/variants are described in detail in all requirements in   EK.10.71.003 Cabin Crew Aircraft Types Manual.  8.3.4. Rapid Deplaning  The rapid deplaning is carried out in cases that are significantly risky but not requiring evacuation and giving sufficient time to disembark the passengers. While the boarding bridge or stairs are still there during/after boarding, and in case of; Fuel spillage, Smoke in the cabin, Fire caused by an accident of the ground support equipment near the aircraft, Accident of other parked aircraft or support vehicles, etc. near the aircraft, or In other cases, not specified herein but deemed necessary by the flight crew, The flight crew may start the rapid deplaning. In such a case, the flight crew make the following announcement:   “Attention, Cabin Crew at Stations” . If the flight crew has decided on the rapid deplaning, the flight crew shall give the following command:   “Attention Cabin Crew, Disembark the Aircraft” . When the flight crew commands the rapid deplaning of the passengers, the Cabin Chief makes the “Rapid Deplaning Announcement” specified in the   Quick Reference Handlist (QRH) and ensures deplaning of all passengers. If the rapid deplaning is not necessary, the flight crew give the following command:   “Cabin Crew and Passengers Remain Seated” . The flight crew may assess the situation and start evacuation instead of rapid deplaning.  8.3.5. Emergency Landing and Evacuation  In order to be ready for any planned/unplanned potential evacuation while they sit at their stations, seatbelt fastened, during landing and takeoff, the cabin crews make the   “SILENT REVIEW”   within the scope of the following items.  O   – Operation of exits  L   – Location of emergency equipment  D   – Drills (e.g., brace for impact)  A   – Able-bodied passengers/PSPs and passengers with reduced mobility  B   – Brace position  C   – Commands Emergency is the process where passengers and crew members are taken away from the aircraft in case of any abnormal situation on ground or in-flight. Various evacuation scenarios may be experienced. Duty of the cabin crew is to evaluate any case of emergency, which may occur, in the best possible way; and to evacuate the passengers from the aircraft as soon and safe as possible. Unplanned emergency Planned emergency  8.3.5.1. Unplanned Emergency  The unplanned emergency occurs without any warning; it gives the crew either very limited time or no time at all to make an action plan. When aircraft accidents are examined, it is observed that the unplanned emergencies generally occur during landing or take off. Therefore, each flight has a critical period of 11 minutes.   “This period includes take-off and the 3-minute period starting as of the take-off, as well as 8 minutes prior to landing and till the aircraft leaves the runway upon landing.”   The cabin crews have to be prepared against any unplanned emergency by carrying out the flight operation implementations fully during every landing and takeoff.  8.3.5.1.1. Unplanned Emergency Commands  In the event that an unplanned emergency occurs when landing is about to take place;  1. Emergency Preparation Checklist  The Emergency Preparation items are available in the   Quick Reference Handlist (QRH) section “1.5. EMERGENCY PREPARATIONS”.  8.3.5.4. Chain of Command  On board aircraft not equipped with Evacuation System; after planned/unplanned landing/ditching, the evacuation command is expected to be given first by the flight crew. In the event that no evacuation command comes from the flight crew, the Cabin Chief or any available Cabin Crew Member shall call the cockpit by interphone. In cases where it is not possible to contact the flight crew, the cabin crew makes sure that the aircraft and the engines have stopped, and first the Cabin Chief gives the evacuation command. In the event that the Cabin Chief cannot give the command, either, each Cabin Crew Member opens the exit(s) for which they are responsible by taking the initiative and starts the passenger evacuation. In the aircraft types equipped with evacuation alert system, the evacuation alert system is operated. The information on the evacuation alert system and its operation is defined in all requirements in   EK.10.71.003 Cabin Crew Aircraft Types Manual. If the Commander or the Co-Pilot cannot give the evacuation command, the cabin crew makes sure that the aircraft and the engines have stopped, and first the Cabin Chief, or if s/he is unable to give commands, the Cabin Crew Members in the cabin give the passengers the commands specified in the Section 8.3.5. Emergency Landing and Evacuation, which commence the evacuation. After passenger evacuation is completed, the Cabin Chief shall enter the cockpit to provide assistance, if necessary.  Selection and Duties of Pre-Selected Passengers (PSP) and Briefing to Them  Pre-selected passengers are selected primarily from deadhead crews or the staff members serving within the organization of the Company. If there is no deadhead crew available on board, persons to be primarily assigned for evacuation as pre-selected passengers are selected from the employees assigned for the flight operation such as designated flying chef, flying service chef other than the cabin crew, the civil servants such as firefighters, police officers, military officers, soldiers, security guards, athletes as per the requirements in  DK.33.001 EASA | Air Operation Regulations CAT.GEN.MPA.115,   DK.22.115 SHT-OPS | Instruction on the Procedures and Principles  for Air Operations ANNEX-4 Commercial Air Transportation (Chapter-CAT) section “Other than cabin crew member”. The cabin crew members select the pre-selected passengers from the sections they are responsible for, and inform them about the exits which they will be assigned to by giving the “PSP BRIEFING” specified in the   Quick Reference Handlist (QRH) Section 1.7. At least two pre-selected passengers shall be selected for each exit. The pre-selected passengers are brought to the exits and given brief information on the opening and use of the exits, the slides/slide rafts and their usage (such as preserving the balance of the slide by holding it by the sides to assist the evacuation) by using the   Safety Card as well, and their feedbacks are received by absolutely making them repeat the actions they will take after every sentence. If no feedback is received from the pre-selected passenger, s/he is not assigned, and s/he is replaced by another passenger. The pre-selected passengers are seated in the places defined in all requirements in EK.10.71.003  Cabin Crew Aircraft Types Manual. Evacuation of the Special Categories of Passengers (SCP) is carried out by the passenger(s) accompanying them, or evacuation of the Special Categories of Passengers (SCP) for whom accompanying passenger is not compulsory (like UM, BLIND, DEAF, etc. passengers) is carried out by the cabin crew after evacuating all passengers from the aircraft. If there is sufficient time before the planned evacuation, the cabin crew gives the accompanying passenger the Accompanying Passenger Briefing available in the Quick  Reference Handlist (QRH) Section 1.7.  8.3.5.5. An infant shall be evacuated in a vertical position where her/his head and neck are being protected by the hand of her/his parent or the accompanier, and where her/his arms and legs are wrapped as much as possible by the other hand of the said person. Evacuation in horizontal positions shall not be preferred, since they may harm the infants. Additionally, in the event that an infant will be evacuated by the help of a second passenger at the overwing exits, the required pre-coordination shall be established in order to ensure a safe evacuation.  8.3.5.8. Evacuation Commands  The evacuation commands are available in all requirements in   EK.10.71.003 Cabin Crew Aircraft Types Manual and the Quick  Reference Handlist (QRH) , depending on the aircraft type.  8.3.5.9. Crowd Control  During an evacuation, primary responsibility of a cabin crew member is to manage passenger evacuation through available exits. The goal is to ensure that passengers and crew members leave the aircraft as soon as possible. In any case requiring evacuation, aircraft may be under an extraordinary situation. Flight crew members shall be aware of the external conditions, which may affect a regular evacuation, and shall inform the cabin crew members in such respect. Positive commands and instructions shall be used while conducting the evacuation. During an emergency evacuation, ensuring that passengers slide one by one from the single lane escape slides, and two passengers slide from dual line escape slides at the same time will guarantee an evacuation completed on time. Cabin crew members shall keep the evacuation progress and status of the slide under surveillance at the station in question. If the circumstances change to render evacuation unsafe to continue further, evacuation shall be stopped and passengers shall be directed to the closest available exit. In the event that passenger(s) trying to get their hand baggage, including also the passengers waiting at the emergency exits with their hand baggage, are detected during evacuation, it is ensured that they leave their hand baggage/belongings in parts of the cabin, which do not prevent the evacuation flow or prevent it only minimally, such as on the seats/zones that are not exit and escape routes, by giving the following command as specified in the   Quick Reference Handlist (QRH) Section 1.11. EVACUATION COMMANDS:  “LEAVE EVERYTHING, COME THIS WAY”  The passengers moving fast toward the door while carrying small bags considered to be not preventing the evacuation or damaging the slide are not stopped; they are allowed to evacuate, and no attempt is made to snatch these bags away from the passengers. The cabin crews take the baggage/item large/heavy enough to be considered to prevent the evacuation and throw them inside the cabin or outside the aircraft (in a controlled way opposite the evacuation direction) in such a manner as not to prevent the evacuation.  8.3.5.9.1. Controlling the Crowd outside the Aircraft after Evacuation  The passengers are guided by using the megaphone so that they gather together at a safe distance outside the aircraft (far from the engines and fuel depots); first aid is provided, if necessary (until the medical personnel come to the scene of incident), and the passengers and equipment are counted if possible.  8.3.5.10. Initiating Evacuation  Make sure that the aircraft and the engines have stopped. The flight crew give the evacuation command in all aircraft types and/or start the evacuation by using the “Evacuation Alert/Signal System” on aircraft with evacuation alert/signal system. If no command/evacuation signal is received from the flight crew, check the external circumstances and open the exit you are assigned to, as specified in the Section 8.3.5.4. Chain of Command, Visually check if the internal and external circumstances are safe. In the event that the Cabin Crew Member is responsible for two doors, the primary exit in case of an unplanned evacuation is the door defined in the “Normal Stations” section of the Cabin Crew Checklist.  a. If the exit can be used;  Depending on the aircraft type and landing type, open the exit and evacuate the aircraft as per the procedures described in  EK.10.71.003 Cabin Crew Aircraft Types Manual , Sections Landing and Ditching. During evacuation; Make sure that passengers wait at a certain distance to the exit, until the slide completely inflates. If you are responsible for two doors, first open the primary exit and start the evacuation, and then go to the secondary exit. Start the evacuation by following the abovementioned steps at the secondary exit as well. Secure yourself in the dedicated assist space by holding the assist handle. If there is a perpendicular surface at your back like panel, lavatory, or galley, pressing the heels and upper back firmly against this surface will help to stand clear of the exit route. Give evacuation command to the passengers. Sound confident and assertive, while giving the commands. The studies have proven that cabin crew members with a confident and assertive attitude affect the passenger evacuation in a positive way. Constantly monitor external circumstances, cabin and the slide, and make sure that the circumstances are suitable; and keep the passenger flow under surveillance. Push the passenger sitting on the slide, reluctant to slide down, from the bottom of her/his waist (not from the knee or shoulder level) to evacuate.  If there is no passenger heading to the exit, you are assigned to, or to the exit on your opposite;  Get passengers to head towards you by calling out positive commands. Remain at your station and continue on observing the circumstances, if required. At the aircraft with class division, the number of passengers seated at the forward section is less, comparing to the intermediate and aft sections. It is necessary to direct the passengers to the forward section by calling out positive commands. Check the cabin and cockpit following the evacuation. After making sure that no one is left, leave the aircraft by taking the materials to be taken in case of evacuation according to the requirements in the section of the relevant aircraft type in EK.10.71.003 Cabin Crew  Aircraft Types Manual.  b. If the exit cannot be used;  Block the exit, and ensure passenger evacuation from the relevant exit; meanwhile, inform the passengers that the said exit is closed.  (Quick Reference Handlist (QRH) Section 1.11. EVACUATION COMMANDS)  "NO EXIT" "NO SLIDE" "FIRE OUTSIDE" "GO THAT EXIT"  First, prevent passenger flow towards the exit out-of-use. Direct the passengers to the other nearest exit available, by standing at the most suitable spot. Visually check if the other exits can be used, and after making sure that those exits are used for passenger evacuation; direct the passengers to the exits in question. Point the exit by your hands and arms while giving commands, in order to direct the passengers to the closest exits. Observe the other exits during evacuation, in order to ensure equal passenger flow through all exits; and direct the passengers to the nearest and most suitable exits that are occupied less. When maximum number of passengers are evacuated from all available exits, and when passenger evacuation is completed simultaneously at each available exit; it indicates that evacuation is achieved at the minimum period of time possible. The following actions shall be taken, if there is no longer a passenger flow towards your exit as the passenger evacuation continues, even though your exit and/or opposite exit is available; Call out strong and positive commands to make the passengers head towards the available exit, for which you are assigned, if necessary; proceed in the aisle and reach the next exit (the one after or before your exit), and ensure that the cabin crew members standing at such exit direct the passengers back to your exit. Continue on observing your exit and keep it under surveillance. If you notice that the passenger flow to an exit close to you is over, direct the passengers waiting nearby to the said exit to ensure a balanced exit strategy. Various evacuation scenarios may be experienced. Duty of the cabin crew is to evaluate any case of emergency, which may occur, in the best possible way; and to evacuate the passengers from the aircraft as soon and safe as possible.  8.3.5.11. Survival  Survival is a struggle to stay alive until rescue arrives. To succeed in this struggle, the rules to be followed by the passengers and crew members after evacuation are listed below; Passengers and crew members shall be kept away from the aircraft to ensure security. The surrounding area shall be searched by taking into account that there might be passengers who walked away under the shock of the accident. The required first aid shall be applied to the injured passengers. It is of great importance to keep the passengers together. The locations to be used as toilet shall be determined. Circumstances shall be evaluated, and in the cases where immediate aid is not expected to arrive, shelters shall be built by use of the slides.  8.3.5.14.1. Factors Affecting Survival  1) Factors Affecting Survival Adversely  Injury Diseases Drought Hunger Hot weather Cold weather Panic Sense of solitude  2) Factors Affecting Survival Positively  Desire to stay alive Being familiar with the region Height of the mountains Rivers-lakes E K . 1 0 . 7 1 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 0 3 C a b i n C r e w M a n u a l QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 186 | Total Page: 298  05045415456216863576102259255250

Rescue Symbols  In case of emergency landing, the ELT is operated immediately after the end of evacuation. Then, it is necessary to send symbols to inform the rescue aircraft about the location and needs. Symbols will be shown by use of branches, trees or grass blocks at any open terrain, or by digging or squashing when the ground is covered with snow. Symbol dimensions shall be at least 25-30 m. The larger and higher the signs are, the larger will their shadows be; and the visibility will be increased. Some of the rescue symbols are indicated below.  Note: Rescue symbols are available in the Emergency Medical Kits and First Aid Kits.  8.3.5.14.3. Basic Survival Rules  1- Protection  Protect the body temperature from hot and cold. Protect the body from dehydration. Keep the chemical balance of the body. Prevent blood loss (first aid).  2- Identification of the Location  Use ELT to the extent possible to allow locating your position. Send rescue symbols.  3- Need for Water  Human body is able to continue fulfilling its functions for 3 weeks without eating. Without water however, loss of consciousness and death are inevitable within 3-11 days. The factors, which may cause dehydration, are listed below; Through urination: Take less fluid, Through vomiting: Take anti-nausea pills, Through respiration: Do not move unless necessary, have rest, E K . 1 0 . 7 1 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 0 3 C a b i n C r e w M a n u a l QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 187 | Total Page: 298  05045415456216863576102259255250
=== Sayfa 190 ===
Through perspiration: Protect yourself from the sun, build a shelter and ensure air circulation inside the shelter, Through swimming: Swimming increases thirst and consumes energy, Though blood loss: Apply first aid.  4- Nutrition  Have your meal before flights. Thereby, you will have the energy for the flight or survival. Since the carbohydrates help the body to retain water, they shall be preferred. Do not consume food containing protein, if there is not enough water. Minimize your need for water. Do not use your energy unnecessarily, protect your bodily fluids; and rest as much as possible. Do not consume fluids for the first 24 hours, you can wet your lips by use of a cotton piece, soaked in water, etc. At the end of 24 hours, drink fluids 3 times a day (morning, noon, evening).  5- Sheltering  Use rafts and slides. Prefer a hill or open terrain.  The persons observing the surroundings must fulfill the following;  Wear life vests. Leave tracks on their way to make it easier to return. Carry axe, rope and sticks.  8.3.5.14.4. Methods For Making Water  Distill the water obtained from rivers, pools or lakes before drinking. If you have the opportunity, prefer drinking the rain water. Do not drink seawater or urine; it will result in delirium or death. Make water by squeezing a piece of clothing dipped in muddy water. Dig a hole 1-2 m farther from the river to make water from a muddy river. The hole will be soon filled with water. If you trace footprints of animals, they will generally lead you to water. While tracing these footprints, be careful not to get lost. Dig a hole in the desert, put the raft canopy or plastic bag in it. Collect the dew formed at the bottom of the plastic. Dew may also be formed on an aircraft wreckage (metal) or plants. Collect the formed dew by use of a sponge, squeeze the sponge in a bowl, and boil the water; it is ready for drinking.  8.3.5.14.5. Huddle Position;  Clinch to each other in the water. Form a tight circle. Minimize your movements. Hug each other around the waist, ensure body contact to the extent possible. Take the elder and injured passengers and infants in the middle of the circle. Clinching forms a block against cold water. It also enables transfer of body temperature and keeps people motivated; and rescue teams can spot the location of passengers more easily.  Regarding Help Position;  Take the position to protect the body temperature. Assume fetal position to occupy a smaller area in water. Pull up your knees towards your chest, and wrap your arms around your legs.  8.3.6. Incapacitated Pilot  If it is found out that a Flight Crew Member is incapacitated during a flight, according to the requirements specified in EK.10.73.001  Operation Manual Part-A,   Section 8.3.14.2 Recognition of Incapacity, the other Flight Crew Member makes the   “PURSER/CABIN CHIEF TO THE COCKPIT”   announcement through the PA and calls the Cabin Chief to the cockpit.” According to the requirements specified in   EK.10.73.001 Operation Manual Part-A,   Section 8.3.14.3 Procedures to be Followed in the event of Incapacitation of a  Flight Crew Member in Flight, the cabin chief shall follow the instructions of the pilot flying and assist the flight crew. a)   Securing Incapacitated Pilot on His Seat:  1- Fasten the safety belt and shoulder harness with arms remaining under the belt. 2- Move the seat of the incapacitated pilot backwards to the extent possible, in order to prevent any damage to the flight controls, buttons/switches, levers. Manner of using seats, as per each aircraft type, is available in all requirements in EK.10.71.003 Cabin Crew  Aircraft Types Manual. 3- Remove the legs of the incapacitated pilot from the pedals. 4- Recline the seat. 5- Lock the safety belt and the shoulder harness. 6- Remove the incapacitated pilot from his seat, if possible, to ensure flight safety and apply first aid; Lift the armrests up. Unfasten the shoulder harness and safety belt. Assistance of at least two (2) persons is needed to take any incapacitated person out of the cockpit without damaging the controls and switches. In line with the requirements in   PR.73.016 Procedure for Cabin Safety in Flights performed with Reduced or No Cabin Crew, article 6.2.2 Cabin Crew, if it is not possible to remove the incapacitated Flight Crew Member from the cockpit with the help of one Cabin Crew Member without damaging the flight controls and buttons on the flights performed with 1 Cabin Crew Member, the incapacitated crew member is not removed from the cockpit; instead, s/he is secured on their seat. However, if there are non- revenue passengers on board the aircraft, and if these passengers meet the requirements specified in   EK.10.73.001 Operation Manual Part-A, Section 8.3. Flight Procedure, it is possible to ask these passengers [first cabin crew, flight crew, or technician, if present] for help). In the event that the flight crew is incapacitated due to deterioration in their health condition or other reasons requiring emergency intervention, the service is interrupted, if necessary, in line with the information provided by the flight crew, the trolleys are secured in the galleys, and landing preparations are started if landing is to be made at the nearest airport. 7- The doctor announcement is made for the incapacitated crew member, and the first aid procedures (Chapter 14. First Aid) are applied. Turbulence  Flight crew shall inform the cabin crew about the turbulence during cruise by switching on seat belt signs. In the event that flight crew has not switched on the seat belt signs during turbulence, then the Cabin Chief shall assess the situation, and shall inform the flight crew through the interphone about the fact that seat belt signs shall be switched on. Within the first 20 seconds, the Turbulence Announcement available in the   Quick Reference Handlist (QRH) is made. The cabin crew shall ensure that the passenger cabin and the other relevant areas are secured. The decision to suspend product and catering offering activities is at the discretion of the Cabin Chief. The flight crew is contacted by interphone every 30 minutes the fasten seat belts lights remain on, upon the directive of the Commander, the Turbulence Reminder Announcement in the   Quick Reference Handlist (QRH) is made, or, if turbulence has ended, fasten seat belts lights are turned off. It must be noted that the aft galley area of the aircraft may feel turbulence more severely than the forward galley area. If turbulence is felt more in the aft galley, the cabin crew will inform the flight crew. If moderate or severe turbulence persists throughout the descent and the announcement “CABIN CREW BE SEATED FOR LANDING” is made while the cabin crew is seated at their stations, the cabin crew must immediately inform the flight crew that the cabin and galleys are not secured for landing. In the event of Moderate/Severe Turbulence, if the cabin crew members cannot reach the crew seats, they secure themselves in the first seat or safe area they find and, if possible, inform the flight crew that the cabin is not ready. Upcoming/anticipated turbulence (light/severe) events (information from SIGMET, PIREPs, IOCC, ATC, etc.) are communicated by flight crew members using cabin crew-flight crew communication procedures. In this case, cabin crew members take immediate safety measures depending on the severity of the turbulence, and the measures taken are reported to the flight crew as soon as possible. Turbulences are divided into three (3) categories depending on their strength and intensity, namely; Light Turbulence Moderate Turbulence Severe Turbulence The levels of turbulence and the signs that can be seen in the cabin are available in Table-18: Turbulence Level Table below.  Table-18: Turbulence Level Table Light turbulence   Moderate turbulence   Severe turbulence  Light turbulence causes light and rhythmic jolts with no discernible change in altitude or attitude of the aircraft. Moderate turbulence causes rapid jolts or sudden impacts. Severe   turbulence   causes   large   sudden changes   in   aircraft   altitude   and   attitude, severe shaking, and severe impacts.  Signs Seen in the Cabin   Signs Seen in the Cabin   Signs Seen in the Cabin  Liquids   in   glasses   vibrate,   but   no   liquid splashes out of the glass. Liquids splash out of glasses. Trolleys are difficult to steer and move. Unsecured items/equipment will fall/fly or hit here and there. Slight difficulty in steering and moving the trolleys. Passengers feel a slight tension in the seat belts. It becomes difficult to walk in the cabin. It becomes difficult to stand without holding on. Passengers feel tension in their seat belts. It is impossible to walk in the cabin. Passengers feel a severe tension in their seat belts.  8.3.7.1. Light Turbulence  During a light turbulence, seat belt signs shall be set in “ON” position by the flight crew. In the event that seat belt warning lights are turned "ON" during cruise, the turbulence announcement is made to the passengers by the cabin crew within the first 20 seconds. The cabin crews check that all passengers are in their seats, that their seat-belts are fastened, that the hand baggage or large and heavy electronic devices such as notebooks, which can cause injuries due to hitting, are switched off and secured, that the galleys are secured, and ensure that the infants are removed from their bassinets, and the infants are secured on the lap of their companions/in infant car seat/infant carrier. The bassinet is demounted from and secured appropriately. The cabin chief is given “OK”. The decision regarding the continuation of in-cabin activities that do not have affect safety, such as catering service, is taken by the Cabin Chief. The Cabin Chief informs the flight crew through interphone that safety of the cabin and the galleys has been ensured, that the turbulence announcement has been made, and the catering service has been continued. If there is a passenger who wants to use the lavatories, the passenger is instructed not to use the lavatory as long as the seat belt warning lights are on and to keep their seat belt fastened until the seat belt warning lights are turned off. However, in case of a compelling reason for the use of the lavatory, the use of the lavatory may be permitted in consultation with the flight crew and with their permission.  8.3.7.2. Moderate Turbulence  In case of an unanticipated or sudden moderate turbulence or a shift from light turbulence to moderate turbulence, the flight crew will flash the seat belt signs twice (2) to notify the cabin crew. If the flight crew notifies through the seat belt warning lights or by interphone that moderate turbulence is happening/will happen, or if the cabin crew sees signs of moderate turbulence, they take the following measures. If trolley service is given in the cabin, the trolley is secured in the trolley compartment, if possible, by pressing the brake pedals. In cases where the galley cannot be reached, the trolley is secured in the cabin by pressing the brakes. Cabin crew members abandon all duties, secure themselves in the first available seat and remain seated until notified by the flight crew or until the seat belt sign goes off. If possible, they announce turbulence to the passenger within the first 20 seconds. Tasks related to product-service offering are terminated. If the Cabin Chief can access the interphone, s/he informs the flight crew by interphone about the status of the passengers, cabin and galleys, that the cabin crew members have buckled up, that the product-service offering has been terminated, and that the turbulence announcement was made, if it was made. Following ending of the turbulence, cabin crew checks on passengers/Cabin Crew Members who are sick/injured or in need of assistance and checks for cabin damage and reports to flight crew by using the interphone. Cabin crew performs the necessary first aid, if required.  8.3.7.3. Severe Turbulence  It is the turbulence occurring at flight altitude and causing major and sudden changes. a) In case of transiting from light/moderate turbulence to severe turbulence, flight crew inform cabin crew by flashing twice (2) seat belt signs that were previously ‘ON’. b) In case of sudden or unanticipated turbulence, the flight crew turns the ‘OFF’ fasten seat belt signs ‘ON’ and gives information to the cabin crew by flashing them twice (2). Service stops immediately in case of severe turbulence. If trolley service is given in the cabin, the trolley is secured in the trolley compartment, if possible, by pressing the brake pedals. In cases where the galley cannot be reached, the trolley is secured in the cabin by pressing the brakes. Cabin crew members abandon all duties, secure themselves in the first available seat and remain seated until notified by the flight crew or until the seat belt sign goes off. Identification cards must be attached to an above-the-waist front part of the outfit so as to be seen easily. If the person rejects to show his/her card, If the person who tries to board the aircraft is suspected of not having an entrance permission, If the person refrains from or hesitates in introducing himself/herself to the flight/cabin crew members, If there is any suspicion of action that will jeopardize the security of the aircraft, if on board, the flight crew, if not on board, the security departments of the airport must be informed immediately about the matter through the agency of the dispatcher and/or station official. e) All employees who embark/disembark the aircraft at the main airports or transit airports shall be carefully monitored, and shall be kept under surveillance. 10.2.4. Crew Baggage Security  a) In Flight  1- Crew members are not permitted to carry packages, baggage, mails (letters, packages, transfer items, etc.) belonging to the other crew members or other persons. 2- The cabin crew members are responsible for security of their own personal belongings.  b) In Airports  1- Keep crew baggage locked and under supervision constantly, 2- Keep away from the unclaimed baggage and do not use mobile phones near them, 3- Do not indicate any address on baggage tags.  c) Other  1- Baggage must always be kept under control and never left unattended at public places such as hotel lounges, lobbies, restaurants, restrooms, etc., 2- During accommodation at the hotels, the room numbers must be kept confidential and while the room is unoccupied, the important documents such as identification cards and passports shall be kept in the locked baggage, 3- Content of the baggage must be checked before leaving the hotel.  10.2.5. Cockpit Security  The procedures for using the cockpit door are implemented as specified in   EK.10.73.001 Operations Manual Part-A, sections 10.1.3 Admission to Flight Crew Compartment, 10.1.4 Flight Deck Door Principles, 10.1.5 Locked Flight Deck Door Procedures, and  PR.70.003 Procedure for Flight Crew Compartment Entry And Exit . The sterile cockpit means that the cabin crew may neither call the flight crew nor enter the cockpit, even for cockpit briefing, at critical phases of the flight and during taxiing, except for the force majeure specified in article 10.2.5.1.b in relation to flight safety, security and the first aid. The procedures related to the subject are explained in  EK.10.73.001 Operations Manual Part-A, Section 8.3.10.4 Sterile Flight Crew Compartment. The cockpit door shall not be left open/half close while entering to/exit from the cockpit as long as the passengers are on board; it must be kept closed at all levels of threat, including the "unruly passengers" case, presence of any sick passenger, etc.  On the ground;  1. The cockpit door is closed and locked just upon boarding of the first passenger at the latest and kept closed and locked until the last passenger leaves the aircraft. Coordination and communication between the cockpit and cabin shall be ensured by use of interphone during such period. 2. No password shall be used while entering to and exit from the cockpit, excluding any emergency. The keypad near the cockpit door shall be used only in case of emergency. 3. After the start of boarding, cockpit entries and exits are kept at the minimum level. No one but the Flight Crew Members is admitted to the cockpit. But, in addition to the flight crew on duty, the persons to be accepted to the cockpit specified in EK.10.73.001  Operations Manual Part-A, Section 8.3.12 Admission to Flight Crew Compartment may be present in the cockpit: 4. In cases where the operational employee must enter the cockpit, the Cabin Crew Member present in the “clear zone” shall take the necessary actions, and the operational employee shall enter the cockpit after the cockpit is called by the “interphone”. While exiting from the cockpit, on the other hand, first the “clear zone” shall be checked through the camera system. 5. In cases where the camera system does not operate or there is no camera system at all, this check shall be made through the observation window on the cockpit door. While exiting from the cockpit, a Flight Crew Member makes a call through the “interphone” and request that the necessary safety measures are taken. 6. There shall be no one waiting in front of the cockpit door except for the Cabin Crew Member required to be there to meet the passengers upon commencement of the passenger boarding and the employee required to be there to carry out the flight operation. If the relevant employee is required to enter or exit the cockpit, the cockpit door shall not be left open after entering or exiting. There is no need to stop boarding or deboarding of passengers during such entries and exits. In the narrow-body aircraft, the check of this zone and welcoming of the passengers shall be made by the Cabin Chief. In the wide-body aircraft, if the passengers are not welcomed at the door “1L”, there shall be one Cabin Crew Member at the “B/C” zone; if the passengers are welcomed at the said door, on the other hand, one Cabin Chief shall be present in the said zone. 7. Before starting the flight briefing, the Commander informs the Cabin Chief that s/he shall give briefing, thus ensuring that the cockpit door is closed, and then, locks the door. In the meantime, the Cabin Chief takes the necessary actions to prevent unnecessary cockpit entry-exit until it is informed by the Commander that the briefing is over in order to prevent interruption of the briefing.  In Flight;  With the exception of the following conditions, the cockpit doors are kept closed and locked during the flight: 1. After the takeoff, depending on the block time and the weather conditions, the “Fasten Seat Belts” lights are turned first “OFF” then “ON” while passing the airport altitude plus 5,000 feet at the earliest, and the Cabin Crew Members are thus enabled to start the service. In accordance with the sterile cockpit practice, the first contact between the flight crew and Cabin Crew Members is established by the Flight Crew Members through the interphone. However, if this contact is not made within 20 minutes following turning “OFF” and “ON” the “Fasten Seat Belts” lights, the Cabin Chief gives the Flight Crew Members information about the cabin safety and the passenger situation by “interphone” at the earliest opportunity. 2. During the first one hour of the flight, entering into or exiting from the cockpit are not allowed except for the compulsory conditions and the communication is ensured through interphone. The Flight Crew Members shall be called by the Cabin Chief through the "interphone" every half an hour during the day flights exceeding 1 hour, and every 20 minutes during the night flights. The Flight Crew and Cabin Crew Members make their requests through the “interphone” system. No password shall be used while entering to and exit from the cockpit, excluding any emergency. The "Keypad" near the cockpit door shall be used only in case of emergency. 3. In cases where it is necessary to give any information or serve foods and drinks by entering the cockpit; The trolley shall be pulled in to the front of the galley/aisle (do not wait at the trolley) and the curtain, if any, is closed in the narrow- body aircraft; the necessary actions are taken in the “clear zone”; and the Flight Crew Members are informed through the “interphone”. The cockpit door shall never be left ajar; it is necessary to make sure to close it immediately after the entry/exit or service. The Curtain is closed in the wide-body aircraft; the necessary actions are taken in the “clear zone”; and the Flight Crew Members are informed through the “interphone”. The cockpit door shall never be left ajar; it is necessary to make sure to close it immediately after the entry/exit or service. In the B777 aircraft, for the purpose of keeping the field of view of the cockpit camera system clear, the curtain in front of the cockpit door, if any, shall be kept open by tying it, and the curtain between the business class and the galley shall be kept closed every time entering and exiting the cockpit. All time, other than cockpit entry/exit, the curtain in front of the cockpit door shall be kept closed. Regarding the flight safety, beverage service shall be performed from the window side of the cockpit, in order to prevent short circuit of devices due to spilled beverages. 4. Any Cabin Crew Member may enter the cockpit, provided that Clear Zone (leaving no passenger in galleys, lavatories, and entrance area in front of the cockpit door, which are all close to cockpit) is ensured before opening the cockpit door during the flight. 5. In case the flight crew consists of two persons during the flight, when one of the flight crew members is required to leave the cockpit for any reason and when one Flight Crew Member will remain in the cockpit, it is not mandatory for any Cabin Crew Member to be in the cockpit within the scope of all requirements specified DK.22.153 UOD-2018/5 Minimum Number of Personnel To Be Found In  Cockpit During Flight, and the requirements specified in   EK.10.73.001 Operations Manual Part-A, Section 10.1.5 Locked Flight Deck Door Procedures and Section 8.3.10 Crew Members at Their Stations are followed. Accordingly; In case of an extraordinary situation, or when s/he needs the other Flight Crew Member, the Flight Crew Member who stays in the cockpit sends 3 chimes from the cockpit to the cabin, turns the seat belt signs ON and OFF repeatedly, or gives information to the cabin crew by interphone. In order to answer any potential call to be made from the cockpit rapidly, a Cabin Crew Member stays in the cockpit entrance area until the other Flight Crew Member returns. When the Flight Crew Members need to leave the cockpit for any reason whatsoever; In narrow body aircraft, before the Flight Crew Member leaves the cockpit, s/he informs the Cabin Chief/Cabin Crew Member on duty on the fore via “interphone”, and the trolley and curtain, if any, is pulled in front of the galley/corridor by the Cabin Crew Member. When the Flight Crew Member who has exited the cockpit wants to enter back the cockpit, s/he enters the cockpit by making a call through the “interphone”. In the wide-body aircraft, it is necessary to keep the curtain closed for safety of the “clear zone”. In B777 aircraft, it is necessary to keep the curtain (if there is one) in front of the cockpit door open and close the curtains between the business class and the galley. When the Flight Crew Members return to the cockpit, it is ensured that the door is opened by giving information to the cockpit through the “interphone”. 6. All entries to the cockpit are checked through the camera system; in cases where the camera system does not operate or there is no camera system at all, the Cabin Chief or an experienced Cabin Crew Member deemed appropriate by the Cabin Chief must stay in the cabin to observe the outside until the Flight Crew Member comes back, as per   EK.10.73.001 Operations Manual Part-A, Section 10.1.5.1 Locked Flight Deck Door Procedures and the following Table-22: Procedures for Entering to/Exiting from Cockpit (Aircrafts without Camera System) table. 7. Entries to cockpit must be kept at minimum level at all phases of the flight, including preparation of the aircraft and staying period in the cockpit shall be minimized (maximum 5 minutes) excluding abnormal situations, emergencies and briefing process of the captain/Cabin Chief. The conversations must be limited with subjects directly concerned with the flight. 8. In order to monitor the “clear zone” through the camera system easily during the night operations, the Cabin Chief shall adjust the “galley” lighting before entry to and exit from the cockpit.  10.2.5.1. Communication between the Flight Crew and the Cabin Crew when the Cockpit Door is locked  (A) Operation with a locked flight deck door shall not inhibit communication between Flight Crew Members and Cabin Crew Members. (B) After locking the cockpit door, the primary channel of communication between the cockpit and the cabin is interphone. (C) If the interphone system does not operate, the crew must determine other means such as video system or entry code to enter the cockpit during the flight. (D) The cabin crew shall use the interphone and/or emergency cockpit warning system to report any suspicious activity or unlawful interference on board the aircraft to the flight crew or enter the cockpit (Airbus). (E) Abnormal communication (depending on the urgency) can be started through the following: (1) Cabin Chief call (or similar system) or (2) "Alarm call" made from the cockpit or cabin (or similar system) or (3) PA call “Cabin Chief to interphone/cockpit”.  10.2.6. Observation of Passengers for Security Purpose and Selection of ABP  a) Crew members must be watchful and careful during boarding, and must not deal with any works, which will hinder to take pre-flight security measures. b) Each passenger boarding the aircraft shall be welcomed carefully in order to identify the passengers to be selected as Able-Bodied Passenger (ABP), and to keep them in mind.  10.2.7. Transportation of Firearms  The rules regarding the carriage of firearms are detailed in   EK.10.73.001 Operations Manual Part-A, Section 9.2 Transport of Weapons, Munitions of War and Munitions of Sport Weapons and Section 10.1.7 Transport of Weapons Onboard the Aeroplane in parallel with all requirements specified in   DK.22.111 National Civil Aviation Security Program (NCASP) and   EK.10.15.001 Security Program. The Company shall carry the weapons of war and munitions of war by air only if this is approved by all states the flight is planned to pass through whose airspaces. It is carried out in accordance with the requirements specified in   DK.33.001 EASA | Air Operations  Regulations CAT.GEN.MPA.155(a),   DK.22.115 SHT-OPS | Instruction on the Procedures and Principles for Air Operations ANNEX-4 Commercial Air Transportation (Chapter-CAT). If this approval is given, the company shall ensure the following in relation to the weapons of war and munitions of war: In accordance with the requirements specified in   DK.33.001 EASA | Air Operation Regulations CAT.GEN.MPA.155(a) and   DK.22.115 SHT-OPS |  Instruction on the Procedures and Principles for Air Operations ANNEX-4 Commercial Air Transportation (Chapter-CAT). (1) They shall be loaded in a compartment inside the aircraft/in the hold, which is inaccessible to passengers during the flight, and (2) If firearms are carried, they shall be carried empty. Before the commencement of a flight, the company shall ensure that the Commander is informed about the details of any weapons of war and munitions of war intended to be carried and the locations of such weapons and munitions on board the aircraft. It is ensured in accordance with the requirements specified in   DK.33.001 EASA | Air Operations Regulations CAT.GEN.MPA.155(a) and DK.22.115  SHT-OPS | Instruction on the Procedures and Principles for Air Operations ANNEX-4 Commercial Air Transportation (Chapter-CAT). Passengers' all kinds of sharp/penetrating objects or firearms or ammunition of the same cannot be admitted to the cabin at any aircraft of the Company, under any circumstances. Cabin crew members inform the flight crew as soon as possible in the event that they identify any person carrying firearms in the cabin. However, any security guards escorting the top governmental officials shall be exceptionally allowed to embark the aircraft as armed. Details and exemptions for the protection of statesmen with guns in the aircraft cabin are defined in all requirements specified in  DK.22.111 National Civil Aviation Security Program and in   EK.10.15.001 Security Program, Section 11.11.1. Permitted Weapon Carriage, and the implementation rules to be considered by the cabin crew are provided below: The armed individuals are not served alcoholic drinks. The Cabin Chief enables the armed individuals on board the aircraft to meet and become acquainted with each other. The entire responsibility for his weapon on board the aircraft belongs to the security guard himself. Principles of Implementation in relation to carrying Weapons of VIP Guards in Civil Aircraft; a) These practices are valid for domestic line flights (Ercan/CYPRUS included) only, b) It does not apply to private protection of senior government officials who are not civil servants in the relevant annex of all requirements specified in   DK.22.111 National Civil Aviation Security Program. c) The practice is valid only for the period of time during which the public officer security guards travel on duty together with the passengers they protect, d) Since they are already on duty throughout the time, they travel together with the passengers they protect, there is no need to request a separate duty order for the security guards, e) The entire responsibility for his weapon on board the aircraft belongs to the security guard himself, f) All transactions of the person who will travel armed inside the aircraft in capacity of security guard shall be made by the Airport Police Directorate VIP Department employee and the ground handling employee. The ground handling employee shall record the security guard, his weapon and flight information (if it is a transfer flight, the personnel shall inform the security guard’s destination airport), g) Since all transactions shall be made in the Airport Police Directorate VIP Department, the ground handling employee working there shall request the security guard’s government agency ID card in addition to his national ID card to match his identity while making the transactions before the flight, h) The ground handling employee must put a mark on the passenger manifest indicating that the security guards whose identities have been authenticated are armed security guards, and inform this to the Cabin Chief and/or the captain pilot, i) The guards are required to carry their weapons on themselves invisibly to the other passengers without bullet in the barrel and magazine in the grip so as not to fire accidentally, or in a locked bag, again without bullet and magazine inside the weapon. These points are valid for the for the abovementioned top government officials' security guards only. The security guards of the government officials other than the abovementioned ones shall not be given such privileges. Cabin crew members shall be responsible for taking the following actions: No alcoholic beverage shall be served to the passengers carrying firearms. The Cabin Chief shall ensure that all passengers carrying firearms are aware of each other. Any security guards carrying firearms must carry their firearms in a manner that they will not be visible. The station official shall inform the Commander and/or the Cabin Chief of the seat number of any passenger carrying firearms. Use of Cabin Crew Stations by Passengers  The principles regarding the use of vacant crew seats on board aircraft when necessary, during Company flights are defined in  PR.02.70.003 Procedure for Use of Vacant Crew Seats in Flight. The manner of use of the cabin crew stations is detailed in the Section 8.2 Cabin Flight Operation Implementations and EK.10.73.001  Operations Manual Part-A, Section 8.3.13 Use of Vacant Crew Seats.  10.2.9. Security Measures for the Hand Baggage Left on Board at Transit Airports  a) In the event that transit passengers stay onboard the aircraft; 1. The passengers who stay onboard the aircraft are counted by the cabin crew. If no reconciliation can be achieved with regard to the count, the station official/airline representative is informed, and the station official conducts a check inside the aircraft by matching the passengers' identity information. 2. EK.10.71.002 Cabin Crew Announcement Manual, Section 4.3. Baggage Reconciliation Announcement is made. Passengers are requested to take and maintain their baggage and the passengers and baggage are matched. 3. At all transit airports where the crew is changed, the baggage reconciliation shall be made by the cabin crew that shall leave the aircraft. 4. Cabin crew members shall search all overhead bins, under the seats, lavatories and any other sections suitable for placing any properties. 5. In case of any non-reconciled baggage, the methods specified in EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual, Section 10.2.11. Unclaimed and Left (Found) Property on Board/Suspicious Object are applied. 6. In the event that “boarding/deboarding check” and “aircraft protection” services are received, the cabin baggage reconciliation and cleaning applications after disembarking passengers at the intermediate station can be performed simultaneously. b) In the event that passengers will leave the aircraft at transit airports, the followings actions shall be taken: 1. Transit passenger announcement shall be made. 2. All passengers shall leave the aircraft with their hand baggage. 3. Cabin crew members shall search overhead bins, under the seats, lavatories and coatrooms upon the disembarkation of all passengers. 4. If there is unclaimed baggage, the flight crew and station official/airline representative shall be informed and the procedures specified in EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual, Section 10.2.11 Unclaimed and Left (Found) Property on Board/Suspicious Object shall be applied. 5. In the event that some of the passengers (MAAS, PRM, etc.) are required to stay on board the aircraft whereas the others are leaving, the measures specified in sub articles 1 and 2 of article a) shall be applied. After the ASSC application, passengers are boarded to the aircraft and counted again (In the case of crew replacement, ASSC application is performed by Cabin Crew Members, who will continue the flight). The number of passengers is notified to the flight crew and station official/airline representative. In respect of connecting flights, the measures specified under the heading of 10.2.10. Security Measures to Be Taken for Passengers Who Embark the Wrong Aircraft or Refuse to Fly After Embarking shall be taken for the passengers, who preferred to disembark the aircraft at the intermediate airport, and who preferred not to continue to the flight. 10.2.10. Security Measures to be taken for Passengers who Embark the Wrong Aircraft/Refuse to Fly After Embarking/Denied Boarding  In the event that any person, who has been admitted as passenger, and who has undergone security checks in accordance with the civil aviation regulations, embarks the wrong aircraft in any way whatsoever, and that such passenger disembarks/is disembarked the aircraft subsequent to the detection of the confusion, or that s/he refuses to fly at the last minute, additional security measures are taken: In the event that the passenger who refuses to fly reverses their decision upon being informed on the security actions to be taken when they disembark, and that the local applications may differ, the cabin crew shall not take any action. If there is any passenger who embarks the wrong aircraft/refuses to fly after embarking; a) Such passengers shall disembark the aircraft with their hand baggage. b) Registered baggage of the passenger, if any, shall be unloaded. c) EK.10.71.002 Cabin Crew Announcement Manual Section 2.16. Passengers who Embarked on Wrong Aircraft/Refuse to Fly announcement is made to the passengers on board and an in-flight security search is conducted so as to cover the places accessible by the passenger who has embarked on the wrong aircraft or refused to fly. d) At the end of the security check, the Cabin Chief fills out   FR.71.0225 Aircraft Security Search Report for Passengers who Embark the  Wrong Aircraft/Refuse to Fly After Embarking/Denied Passenger, which is obtained from the Cabin Operations Control Supervisory, in two (2) copies. One copy of the form shall be submitted to the station official at domestic stations, and to the station official at outstations. The second copy of the form is delivered by the Cabin Chief to the Cabin Operations Management. e) In the event that the unclaimed items/objects found during the search and check of the cabin meet the suspicious objects description (i.e., they are suspicious objects), actions are taken as per the methods defined in EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual, Section 10.2.11. Unclaimed and Left (Found) Property on Board/Suspicious Object.  10.2.11. Unclaimed and Left (Found) Property on Board/Suspicious Object  The first assessment of the property/object found by the cabin crew during the cabin check is made visually by the person who has found it without touching it or changing its location, and the Cabin Chief and the Commander are informed of it.  Unclaimed and Left (Found) Item:  The valuable properties like bag, wallet, jewelry, electronic appliances (mobile phone, tablet, laptop, video camera, camera, electronic book, music player, earphone, game console) and valueless properties such as cabin baggage, book, garment, umbrella, eyeglasses, keyring, neck pillow, magazine, personal accessories, imitation jewelry, and hairpin, which have been left at the locations that are either owned or rented by the Company, on board the Company aircraft and not taken back by their owners, “not considered suspicious object”, either. If the property/object is deemed unclaimed and left (found) property, the methods to be applied for such object are described in accordance with the requirements specified in   EK.10.67.001 Ground Operations Manual (GOM), Section 2.9.5.1.Found Properties and as per   TL.67.032 Unclaimed and Forgotten (Found Items) Item Properties Processes. For each found property,   FR.67.0144 Found Property Release Form must be filled out in detail together with C/A1, and delivered to the lost property official or the station official inside the aircraft. One copy of this form completed is retained by C/A 1 to deliver urgently to Cabin Crew Directorate, while the other copies are retained by the ground personnel.  Suspicious Object:  Properties, objects, packages and/or all the electronic devices that appear to be tampered, the contents of which cannot be seen and/or identified clearly through external visual check, which emit sounds and/or odors, which vibrate and/or leak fluids, which cables, ropes/strings, etc. stick out from, Toys that have mechanisms and are convenient to place item(s) inside in terms of their features and physical structures,   packages, items, and objects that raise the suspicion of being left intentionally and are not regarded as Unclaimed and Left (Found) Item. Note-1: Since the electronic devices that are shorter than 16 cm, narrower than 9 cm, thinner than 1.5 cm according to the dimensions determined by the international security authorities and have no signs of tampering are not subjected to the necessary security measures on the grounds that they are not suspicious; if they are detected during the flight, continuation of the flight is deemed appropriate. Note-2: If the items like bags, wallets, mobile phones, etc. neither emit sounds, odors nor vibrate nor leak fluids, they are regarded as “Unclaimed and Left (Found) Item” within the scope   TL.67.032 Unclaimed and Forgotten (Found Items) Item Properties Processes.
