14.26. General Rules required to be observed during Travel  The following are the most important steps to take to protect personal and public health: (i) obtain information about the health conditions and the possible disease risks in the country to be traveled under assignment from the R.O.T. Ministry of Health Directorate General of Health for Border and Coastal Areas “Travel Health Center” internet site and/or call center or our health offices; (ii) start the suggested protective tablet treatment on time; and (iii) be vaccinated.  General Rules You Are Required to Observe During Travel  Remember that learning the conditions peculiar to the region to be traveled and the health measures to be taken before going to travel is very important for a healthy travel. Wash your hands with water and soap frequently. Absolutely boil the waters that are not safe to drink. Do not forget that ice may also be dirty in the places where water may be dirty, and do not put ice into drinks. Do not brush your teeth with tap water in places where water may be dirty. Do not eat the food which you suspect of its freshness and whether it has been boiled or not. All raw or inadequately cooked-food carry the risk of being dirty. Abstain from eating such food. Remember that consuming the street-vended food and drinks increase the risk of being infected with such disease. Pay attention to expiry dates of all foods sold as packaged. Since swimming in and contacting the waters that are suspected to be unclean may cause various diseases, make sure not to swim in pools and sea waters that you suspect to be unclean. Take all required measures against insects. It will be helpful to use fly-repellent sprays, sleep with mosquito net and wear long- sleeved garments and trousers. Avoid unprotected sexual intercourse. Avoid from contacting with especially cats, dogs and monkeys; in the event that you are bitten or injured by such animals, then apply to medical authorities as soon as possible. In the event that you apply to any healthcare provider due to any reason, make sure that the syringes used for you are disposable and the equipment are sterile.  14.27. Working at High Altitudes  Working in a pressurized cabin at high altitudes for long hours may be rather tiresome. In addition to being responsible for the passengers' safety, the cabin crew members have to give the passengers the top-quality service within the limited time period. Working in small galleys, pushing and pulling heavy trolleys, and lifting heavy objects may lead to locomotor system diseases and injuries. Disturbance to body balance caused by flying between different time zones, irregular sleep and eating, fatigue, dealing with angry passengers, breathing the air circulating continuously in the cabin, being exposed continuous noise and vibrations, and the changing climatic conditions may challenge the crew members.  14.27.1. Altitude Physiology  Anatomy of the human body is not suitable for living at high altitudes. Environmental changes incurred during the flight are pressure and temperature differences, low humidity rate, and the three-dimensional movement at high velocity. Human body requires receiving oxygen at a certain level continuously. Oxygen is brought to the cells and tissues of the body through blood circulation. Due to changes in atmospheric pressure, as the person gets higher and higher from the ground level, the concentration of the gas molecules decreases, and so does the oxygen level. Besides, as the altitude increases, the gas molecules expand.  14.27.2. Physiological Effects  Although the oxygen level inside an aircraft cabin is lower, this can be tolerated by healthy individuals easily. However, low oxygen level inside the cabin may affect the individuals suffering from cardiopulmonary and/or blood diseases. Additionally, expansion of the gases in E K . 1 0 . 7 1 . 0 0 1 | R e v i s i o n 0 3 C a b i n C r e w M a n u a l QMS Document Template Number: FR.18.0001 | Revision 12 Document Template Reference Document Number: TL.18.006 Page: 267 | Total Page: 298  05045415456216863576102259255250

the body cavities may lead to discomfort, indigestion and gas pains. Flying with inflamed and congested ears, nose and sinuses causes pain and even barotrauma in the ears especially during ascent and descent. Since the rate of humidity in the air circulating in the cabin is just 10%, this leads to dehydration and dryness in the body. Another adverse effect suffered by the passengers and the crew members is the nausea and illness caused by the continuous noise and vibration.  14.27.3. Cosmic and Solar Radiation  The solar radiation is the radiation coming from the Sun to the World. The cosmic radiation, on the other hand, is the radiation coming to us from the other stars. Although the shortwave rays of the Sun warm our World, the longwave rays such as the Gamma rays have radiative effect. The ozone layer decreases this effect. However, during the high-altitude travels, the people are at the upper part of the ozone layer, and thus, exposed to more radiation.  14.27.4. Factors Influencing the Dose of Radiation We take during Flight  BLOCK TIME:   The committed dose is directly proportional to length of the block time. We shall pay more attention to our health measures before and after the long-haul flights.  LATITUDE:   The higher the latitude, the higher the radiation value.  ALTITUDE:   The higher the altitude, the higher the exposed radiation dose, because the protective atmospheric layer above you is thinner.  SOLAR ACTIVITY:   In consequence of the solar activity, the radiation level either increases or decreases depending on the month. Solar storms happen at certain intervals. At such times, the level of the radiation we will be exposed to on board the aircraft due to sun is the maximum.  14.27.5. Radiation Degree and Its Calculation  The radiation measurement unit is Sievert (Sv). This radiation degree, which is 1.5 Sv at sea level, varies by the electromagnetic order of the world. The radiation degree increases from south to north. The North Pole contains three times more radiation than the South Pole. The highest level of radiation on the Earth is on the 60th northern latitude. In order calculate the in-flight radiation exposure level, The following formula shall be used: 52 Sv x Total Number of Days Flown a Year / 365. For example, this figure is 40 days a year over 80 hours on average a month.  52x40/365 = 5.69 Sv  As can be seen, the level of in-flight radiation we are exposed to is rather low. In Europe, the flight and cabin crew members are warned to take additional measures if they are exposed to radiation above   6 Sv . Since we fly for maximum 1,000 hours a year, this level will be limited to maximum   5.93 Sv   a year.  14.27.6. Potential Measures to take to mitigate the Radiation Effect  Take a shower after flight:   By taking a shower after the flight, we get rid of the radiation on the body surface, and diffuse the absorbed radiation in the body.  Consume vegetables and fruits rich in antioxidants : The antioxidants prevent the DNA breakage. If these breakages are not prevented, cancer formation in the cell may be observed (Orange, Green tea, Tomato, Garlic, Soybean…).  Take group B vitamins and foods containing Potassium:   Green vegetables, Fruits, Muskmelon, Watermelon…  Milk Products and Yogurt:   They do not protect from radiation, but are very useful in renewal of the cells and tissues damaged by radiation.  Sports:   Sedentary life without sports increases any cancer risk. The change of the climate in the world is not equal in the whole world and every individual reacts differently. Contagious Diseases  General Ways of Protecting from All Infectious Diseases:  Close your mouth and nose with a paper napkin while coughing or sneezing. Throw the paper napkins into the bin immediately after you have used them. Rinse your hands with ample water and soap after coughing or sneezing. It is recommended that you shall rinse your hands for at least 15-20 seconds. Alcohol-based hand sanitizers can also be preferred. Avoid touching your mouth, nose and eye with your dirty hands. All infectious diseases, especially viral diseases, may be transmitted by means of shaking hands/contact with other people. Avoid getting into close contact with the patients of such disease. Take care of your health. Sleep well, make physical exercises, abstain from stress, consume ample amount of fluids and eat well. It is necessary to keep social distancing wherever possible. It is necessary to pay attention to hand hygiene. The hands shall be washed with water and soap for minimum 20 seconds frequently, or in case of absence of water and soap, alcohol-based hand sanitizer shall be used. Even if the mask is worn, the mouth and nose shall be covered with a paper tissue or the upper part of the arm if there is no paper tissue while sneezing or coughing. It is necessary to take as much care as possible to not touch the surfaces directly. Wearing gloves cannot substitute washing the hands regularly and thoroughly. The gloves shall not be worn for too long. After they have been taken off, the gloves shall not be worn again. After taking off the gloves, it is necessary to wash the hands with water and soap, or disinfect them with alcohol-based hand sanitizer. It is necessary to take care to not touch nose, mouth, and eyes with hands. COVID-19 Disease  Coronaviruses constitute a large viral family that can cause diseases in animals and humans. It is known that several coronaviruses cause respiratory tract infections in humans, ranging from common cold to much severer Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) and Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS). On 31 December 2019, China informed the World Health Organization of the pneumonia cases in Wuhan city of Hubei province, the etiology of which was unknown. On 7 January 2020, the factor was defined as a new coronavirus (2019-nCoV) that was not found in humans previously. Then, the name of 2019-nCoV disease became COVID-19; and the viral factor was named SARS-CoV-2 due to its resemblance with SARS CoV. Coronaviruses constitute a large viral family that can cause diseases in animals or humans. It is known that several coronaviruses cause respiratory tract infections in humans, ranging from common cold to much severer diseases like Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) and Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS). The COVID-19 virus causes the coronavirus disease.  Symptoms:  It has been observed that the average incubation period is 5-6 days (2-14 days), but can rise to 14 days in certain cases. The exact contamination period of COVID-19 is not known. It is thought that it starts 1-2 days before the symptomatic period and ends when the symptoms disappear. The most prevalent symptoms of COVID-19 are fever, dry cough, and fatigue. Some   other   less   prevalent   symptoms   observed   in   certain   patients   include   muscle-joint   pain,   nasal   congestion,   headache, conjunctivitis, sore throat, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, loss of taste or smell, skin redness, or color change in the fingers and toes. The symptoms are generally light and appear slowly. Some people get infected, but can pull through the disease with very light symptoms or no symptoms at all. Most of the people (almost 80%) recover without needing a treatment. Approximately 1 out of every 5 persons who have caught COVID-19 becomes seriously ill and has difficulty in breathing.   Old people and those who have underlying diseases like hypertension, heart and lung problems, diabetes, or cancer are under the risk of developing a severe disease. However, everybody can catch COVID-19 and become severely ill.   The people of all ages who suffer from shortness of breath, chest pain/pressure, fever, difficulty in speaking, loss of mobility and/or cough are recommended that they receive medical assistance.  How does it infect?  It is thought that the disease has a zoonotic origin, and the viral factor can be transmitted from the patients to the other people. It is transmitted from person to person through the droplets sputtered when the patient coughs, sneezes, or talks. The people who are close to an infected person can catch COVID-19 by inhaling these droplets in the air. Therefore, it is important to stay at least 1 meter away from the other people. Besides, since these droplets are relatively heavy, they cannot float in the air for long, and drop on the objects and surfaces around the person, such as table, door handle, and handrails quickly. The information obtained on the COVID-19 infection so far indicates that some people are at higher risk of becoming ill and developing severe symptoms. 80% of the patients have the disease lightly. 20% of the patients are treated in hospital. What are the Ways of Protection?  The most important way of protection is vaccination. Several different types of vaccines have been developed for COVID-19. All these vaccines have been designed to teach the immune system of the body how to know and destroy the virus that causes COVID-19 safely. The vaccines that contain inactive virus that does not cause the disease but leads to immune response (inactive vaccines). The vaccines that contain attenuated virus that does not cause the disease but leads to immune response (live attenuated vaccines). The protein-based vaccines that use the pieces of protein that imitate the structure of the COVID-19 virus to lead to immune response safely. The viral vector vaccines that carry the RNA pieces of the COVID-19 virus and use the viruses that cannot cause the disease, in order to lead to immune response safely. The m-RNA and DNA vaccines that are the state-of-the-art approach that uses the RNA and DNA pieces designed to produce the protein that leads to a safe immune response alone. There is no need to use antiseptic or antibacterial soaps; normal soap is sufficient. Hepatitis  Hepatitis may be transmitted by viruses, chemical substances, alcohol and medicines; it may be seen in liver-gallbladder diseases, as well. There are 3 types of hepatitis:  a) Hepatitis A (viral or infectious):   It is generally encountered with such type in children. Symptoms may not be seen in Hepatitis A- infected children. Such patients may transmit the disease to their parents (especially in such close contacts as changing the babies' diapers). Hepatitis A does not create severe disorders and the patients generally recover without having difficulty. People may be infected with Hepatitis A through contaminated water and by consuming raw or inadequately-cooked marine products.  b) Hepatitis B (serum):   It is transmitted by contact and mixture with other blood (blood transfusion, injection), contact with saliva and phlegm or sexual intercourse. It can survive for a long time under environmental conditions owing to the fact that it is a durable virus. It can survive on the infected surfaces for 6 weeks or longer. It may be difficult to identify the patient of Hepatitis B from the external symptoms. Many patients maintain their lives without any symptoms. Such cases are called latent infections and such patients are called latent carrier.  Symptoms: Vomiting, weakness, stomachache and jaundice. Many patients who have only the symptoms of “Flu” are not noticed generally. Incubation period of Hepatitis B is a long period such as 42-200 days. The patients of such disease may be affected severely in long term. Many patients are carriers and such disease may become chronic in these patients. It has been proved that Hepatitis B is associated with liver cancer. It does not have a specific treatment. Therefore, risk groups shall be protected by means of vaccination.  Ways of Protection: It is indicated that the most effective way of protection against Hepatitis is vaccination. Rinse your hands well and thoroughly. Use disposable gloves if you will contact with blood or mouth secretions. Clean blood-contaminated places and devices with universal precaution kit on board. Hide the used injector needles appropriately and put them in the medical waste box in the Emergency Medical Kit if there is a physician, or in the medical waste box in the First Aid Kit if there is no physician.  c) Hepatitis Non A-Non B (transfusion):   Its symptoms are similar to the symptoms of the other types. It is transmitted by blood transfusion and contaminated (infected) needles. The reason why it is called Non A-Non B is the lack of relevant laboratory tests to identify the virus.  14.28.3. Meningitis  Viral or bacterial inflammatory disease of the cerebral cortex. Viral meningitis is transmitted by food and water. Bacterial meningitis is transmitted by the intake of secretions from mouth to mouth, especially while the patient is coughing to your face in the course of first aid treatment. Do not forget to be vaccinated against meningitis every 5 years regularly in order to protect yourself, especially in the flights to Saudi Arabia where meningitis epidemics may break out during Hajj visits. 14.28.4. Tuberculosis (Phthisis)  Tuberculosis is developed when the microbe called mycobacterium tuberculosis settles in such body parts as lung, bones, kidney, intestines, lymph node. Tuberculosis may lead to diseases in all organs, especially lungs. It may be fatal if left untreated or treated improperly. Tuberculosis microbe settles in lungs. Main symptoms of the disease are coughing, expectorating phlegm, weight loss, loss of appetite, fever, night sweating and expectorating blood while coughing. Coughing is the most common and important symptom; therefore, if any person coughs for more than 3 weeks, s/he shall go to the nearest tuberculosis dispensary.  14.28.5. AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome)  Human immune defect virus (HIV) is the cause of AIDS. It has been discovered in 1983. HIV attacks to the white blood cell (T4 lymphocytes) of the immune system and destroys them. Loss of these cells by any persons infected by HIV eases occurrence of illness due to the organisms (opportunistic microorganisms), which do not cause such illnesses under normal conditions. The virus, which is not durable to the outer environment, cannot survive outside the body to be able to create a disease. It is easy to kill it with disinfectants used under direct sunshine and in dry environments.  Transmission  It may be transmitted by infected blood, semen or infected body fluids. Blood transfusion is one of the most important risks. It may be transmitted from the infected mothers to the babies via placenta; however, it has been observed that pregnant women who have strong immunity against this disease and high levels of serum T lymphocyte (CTL) do not transmit AIDS to their babies. It is rare but possible that HIV infection may be transmitted by means of human bites.   It has not been proved with medical documents that HIV infection is  transmitted by means of tear, sweat, saliva, phlegm, urine, stool, vomit or nasal discharge (unless they contain excessive blood).  CAUTION:   AIDS is not transmitted by means of shaking hands, kissing, toilet covers, telephones, bathtubs or mosquitoes.  Protection  Wear gloves every time you do first aid. Use protective gloves like rubber gloves while cleaning contaminated materials and equipment. If possible, use thick leather gloves or industrial gloves in cases such as taking the patient out from damaged car after a car accident. Use mask or eye protector in cases where the body fluids may spurt out. Preserve the used injections in prick-resistant boxes and do not try to insert them into their covers. Because pinprick cases generally occur while trying to insert the injections into their covers. Apply the protocols for hygiene and protection against infection. Wear scrubs or coveralls in cases where uniforms may be contaminated with the body fluids. Change your contaminated cloths and wash your skin. Use face protectors, pocket masks or other additional protective materials. Rinse your hands in order to protect yourself after taking the gloves off. Intravenous use of drug carries high risk of HIV transmission. Be more careful while applying first aid treatment to the persons suspected of being drug addicts.  14.28.6. Malaria  Necessary Information Regarding Malaria  According to the requirements specified in Causes and Symptoms article of   DK.21.079 Malaria Case Management Guide, malaria is a disease   caused   by   5   (five)   species   of   Plasmodium   parasite   (Plasmodium   Falciparum,   Plasmodium   Vivax,   Plasmodium   Ovale, Plasmodium Malariae and Plasmodium Knowlesi), and leads to death if not treated. Malaria risk may vary depending on the region, the height, and the season, but it is seen mostly in tropical regions (Africa, Asia and Latin America). The information on the incidence of the disease is followed on CDC website:   http://www.cdc.gov/malaria/, FAA website: Federal Aviation  Administration (faa.gov), WHO website:   http://www.who.int/malaria/en/. LS.35.042 List of Countries with Malaria Risk is updated per the information obtained from these sources. Additionally, according to the requirements specified in   DK.49.019 World Malaria Report, prepared by WHO based on information from 84 countries where malaria is endemic, provides a comprehensive and up-to-date trend assessment of malaria control and elimination worldwide. Accordingly, the Company implements necessary updates on malaria prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and surveillance. There is no malaria vaccine. Personal protection against mosquito bites is the first step of defending against malaria. Mode of Transmission  As stated in article Transmission of   DK.21.079 Malaria Case Management Guide, it is transmitted by the bites of infected female anopheles mosquitoes. Other than mosquito bites, the disease is also transmitted through blood transfusions, transplantations, shared syringes, or passed from mother to fetus.  Incubation Period  Parasites causing malaria become full-blown in the liver of human. Incubation period varies from species to species,   but symptoms are seen 7 days at the earliest (generally between 7 and 30 days) after the mosquito bite.   Do not rule out the fact that the incubation period may be rarely prolonged up to 1 year.  Symptoms  Common   symptoms   of   the   malaria   are   as   follows:   fever,   trembling,   sweating,   headache,   stomachache,   myalgia,   muscle weakness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and cough.   Such symptoms of malaria may be confused with the other upper respiratory infections especially the cold in general. These symptoms may be repeated periodically.  Risks  The malaria is seen on a wide area specified in LS.35.042 List of Countries with Malaria Risk and covering especially Africa, Central and South America, parts of the Caribbean, Asia (including South Asia, Southeast Asia and Middle East), Eastern Europe and South Pacific. Frequency of the illness, type of malaria, season, characteristics of the area visited (urban, rural, altitude, etc.), accommodation type (air conditioned or indoors, outdoors), visit duration, personal protective measures and the way of behavior are the main factors in terms of the transmission of malaria. Children, pregnant women and elders are under more risk.  Rules to be observed by Employee to visit Risky Regions Things to do before going to Risky Regions  It is checked whether there is a risk of malaria disease in the destination country and FR.35.0858 Malaria Information Card is kept on flights to all countries. Since there is the risk of having the disease again, the person(s) traveling shall be aware of that they have to take the protective measures against the disease again, even if they had malaria before. IHL Crew Terminal Health department shall be resorted to acquire information about the disease and the country to be visited and the malaria disease personal protective equipment no later than one or two days before flying to the regions included in LS.35.042 List of Countries with Malaria Risk. Those who wish to use preventive medication apply to the IHL Crew Terminal Health department 2-15 days in advance or before the flight at the latest, depending on the medication to be used. You shall take long-sleeved t-shirts, trousers, cotton clothing covering arms and legs with you for your flights to risky region. It is recommended that Flight and Cabin crews wear long-sleeved shirts as uniforms. For flight and cabin crews, information on Malaria prevention and control measures is provided by the commander and/or cabin chief during pre-flight and post-flight briefings.  Things to do while staying in Risky Regions  Malaria transmission takes place mostly between the dusk and the dawn since the anopheles feeds during the night. Take all required precautions against mosquito bites especially at nights; Wear long-sleeved t-shirts, cotton clothing covering arms and legs. Apply the fly-repellent sprays to the parts of your skin exposed to mosquitoes periodically and in compliance with the user's manual of such sprays. If sun-protection cream is going to be applied, apply first the sun-protector and then the fly-repellent on your skin. Throughout the time you are in risky regions, you are required to avoid being outdoors. Especially the regions with high exposure risk such as rural areas, swamps/marshes shall be avoided. Eat your meals in the indoor areas of the hotel. MERS-CoV (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus) Disease  MERS-CoV is a virus that causes severe respiratory tract disease and is communicated from person to person. It is necessary to take the following precautions to be protected from the disease: Take personal protective measures and observe the sanitary rules. Use mouth cover masks in crowded places, if necessary. Avoid close contact with the animals. Do not consume raw milk and animal products (camel-originated products in particular). Wash the vegetables and fruits to be consumed raw thoroughly before eating. Wash your hands frequently with soap and water; if soap and water are unavailable, use alcohol-based hand sanitizers. Avoid touching mouth, nose and eyes, which are the courses of contagion of the virus. Clean and disinfect the surfaces and items likely to be contaminated by the microorganisms. Avoid close contact with infected persons. If you are diagnosed with this disease, avoid contact with other people to the extent possible to prevent contagion. Use a tissue to cover nose and mouth while sneezing or coughing. Throw the used tissue into the trash bin; if you do not have any tissue, cover your nose and mouth with the inner side of your arm while sneezing or coughing. The people who observe lower respiratory tract disease symptoms (cough, shortness of breath) together with fever in themselves within 14 days following their visits to regions with Mers-CoV risk (Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain, Yemen, Lebanon, South Korea and Iran) shall seek medical assistance immediately and give information to the physician attending them on their travels. In case of a suspicious situation; Inform the Cabin Chief and the Commander about the situation in order that the necessary actions are taken without delay. Receive medical support from the ground and/or the medical employee onboard the aircraft, if possible. In such a case, the crew members shall act in accordance with the directives of the medical employee. If you cannot receive any medical support; empty the last two rows of the relevant section of the aircraft, seat the patient there, and isolate him/here from the other passengers. Do not permit other passengers to use the seat emptied by the sick passenger, unless you are sure that the seat has been disinfected. Zika  It is a disease caused by the Zika virus that is a RNA virus from the flaviviridae family, and going around through biting of mosquitoes. Its symptoms may be fever, headache, eye redness, rash, and muscle and joint pains. Generally, it has a mild form and may last for 4-7 days. This disease has no vaccine, no preventive medication. In order to prevent the infection, personal protection against mosquito bites is the first step of defense. Wear long-sleeved t-shirts, gloves, cotton clothing covering arms and legs. Apply the fly-repellent sprays to the parts of your skin exposed to mosquitoes. Throughout the time you are in risky regions, you shall avoid being outdoors unless necessary. Eat your meals in the indoor areas of the hotel. It is appropriate to use mosquito net, if available, and keep the air- conditioner on in the hotel room.  14.28.9 Long Term Cough  Cough continuing for a long time is not itself a disease. However, it can be a symptom of any disease. Its reasons and risk factors may include smoking, chronic bronchitis, dryness of the mouth, allergic diseases, lung cancer, and infections. The disease shall be diagnosed and treated as soon as possible.  14.29. Vaccines  Vaccination is the most commonly applied method in order to protect from infectious diseases and to prevent diseases to spread and cause epidemic outbreaks.  Points to be taken into consideration when being vaccinated:  Individuals who suffer from any suddenly-developed infectious disease, Individuals who still suffer from any suddenly-developed infectious disease or prolonged disease, who still receive medical treatment and who take medicine(s), Pregnant or breastfeeding mothers shall consult to their physicians before being vaccinated.  Vaccines Applied as Protective Methods and Their Protection Periods :  Tetanus vaccine : After the 4 doses of toxoid vaccine administered to the children during their infancy, the 5th dose is administered between the 4 and 6 years of age, and repeated every 10 years after that. Adults shall be vaccinated against tetanus every 5-10 years in order to protect themselves from the risk of tetanus in injuries and burns. Proper Storage, Carriage and Disposal of Medical Wastes  Medical waste generated after the use of the Emergency Medical Kit and the First Aid Kit on board the aircraft is disposed of in the yellow medical waste bag in these kits; in case of the use of sharp instruments in the Emergency Medical Kit, the sharp instrument in the kit is thrown into the medical waste bin, and the waste bin is closed tightly. The yellow medical waste bags used in flight are sealed and placed in the Emergency Medical Kit and First Aid Kit. The Emergency Medical Kit is not opened for the needle tip medical waste generated after passengers’ personal insulin use. It is ensured that the used needle tips are kept in the passenger’s own personal insulin needle box. Medical waste generated after the use of the universal precaution kit is placed in the red colored biological waste bag in the kit. At the end of the flight, the red colored medical waste bag used is handed over to the ground employee or the station official of the landing airport as sealed. The sharp wastes are collected, separately from the other medical wastes, in the boxes or containers made of plastic or laminated cardboard that has the same features with plastic, which are water-resistant and impervious, tamper-resistant, puncture-, tear-, break-, and burst-resistant, and bear bearing black “INTERNATIONAL BIOHAZARD” symbol and the warning “CAUTION! SHARP MEDICAL WASTE” written in black letters. On board the aircraft, Medical Waste Box is in the Emergency Medical Kit. These accumulation containers are filled to a maximum of ¾ full, sealed, and placed in medical waste bags. Once the sharp waste containers are full, they cannot be compressed, opened, emptied, or recycled. If the medical waste box in the Emergency Medical Kit is full, the box is sorted at the health unit.  Figure-30: International Biohazard Symbol  14.31. Disinfection and Disinsection of Aircraft  Disinfection (Extermination of Bacteria): Processes of exterminating or inactivating the harmful microorganisms through appropriate chemicals in order to prevent the communicable diseases from entering and spreading over our country through vehicles and/or customs zones. Disinsection (Extermination of Insects): Processes related to the health measures taken for controlling or exterminating the insect vectors that are present in vehicles and/or customs zone and cause human diseases.  Disinfection and Disinsection Practices Disinfection  When aircraft disinfection is required, the following provisions apply: The application shall be limited to the container or compartment of the aircraft that carries out the traffic Disinfection is carried out by procedures that comply with the aircraft manufacturer and WHO recommendations; In disinfection of the aircraft, the surface disinfectant approved by SMI (Scientific Material International) and approved by Technical Directorate to be used in the aircraft is used. In accordance with the requirements specified in   DK.31.027 ICAO Annex 9 |Facilitation Chapter 2 article E.   Disinfection of Aircraft, States Parties to the Convention shall ensure that, in the event of contamination of aircraft surfaces or equipment with any bodily fluid, including feces, contaminated areas and used equipment or instruments shall be disinfected. Disinsection Practices  The stations where disinsection is mandatory before landing-takeoff while entering the country report to the health authority of the relevant country. Periodic Residual Disinsection Practice  Flammable chemical compounds or solutions that are likely to damage the aircraft structure, e.g. by corrosion, shall not be used. The disinsection certificate is valid for 8 weeks (56 days), and in case of any incident, disinsection is applied before the certificate expires or after each deep cleaning service. Disinsection is carried out by the contracted service provider at Istanbul Airport, Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen Airport, Ankara Esenboğa Airport, Antalya Airport, and Izmir Adnan Menderes Airport. The information of the newly purchased aircraft is sent by e-mail to the contracted service provider by Ground Operations Directorate. Disinsection is carried out with tools with a spray mechanism. The active ingredients currently recommended by WHO for use in aircraft disinfection are d-phenothrin and permethrin (cis/trans ratio 25/75). Chemicals approved by SMI (Scientific Material International) are used. The first application is carried out by 0.5 g/m2 on carpets and 0.2 g/m2 on all other surfaces including cargo and baggage compartments, in such a way as to leave a residue. The subsequent applications are carried out by 0.2 g/m2 on carpets and 0.1 g/m2 on all other surfaces including cargo and baggage compartments. The air conditioning system shall be turned off during disinsection, and the application area shall be ventilated for at least 1 (one) hour 5 (five) minutes after the application. More attention is paid to the application in cabinets, lavatories, toilet seats, crew rest areas, and other closed compartments where insects are likely to be present. Abdominal Diseases 14.32.1. Stomach Diseases  Stomach is located in the upper left quarter of the abdominal region and protected mostly by the lower left ribs. All reactions occurring as a result of poisoning or trauma led to the stomach muscles to stop and cause the food stay inside the stomach for a long time. Gastritis and Ulcer: Ulcers in the stomach may lead to bleeding. In mild gastric bleeding cases, brown like coffee grounds and stinky blood comes out of the mouth. In severe gastric bleeding cases, light red blood comes out of the mouth. Stool is in dark black color. Gas Pain: The pain caused by accumulated gas is generally arises from the digestive system problems. Mostly, it is an abdominal sickness and rarely causes chest pain. When it causes chest pain, that pain scares and worries the person, because it is thought that it might be related to the heart. The chest pain caused by gas accumulation is generally a short-time but compressive pain. It causes unintended belching. It may also cause simultaneous distention, indigestion, hiccup, nausea, and sometimes vomiting. The gas-related chest pain may be caused by fiber-rich food, food intolerances, or digestive problems. The best and easiest solution is to be careful about the foods consumed. It is more appropriate to eat slowly and chew the food thoroughly, and eat less but more frequently instead of rich meals. Fatty foods and fiber-rich foods (the foods like bean, cabbage, broccoli, dry prune, apple, pear shall be decreased, and gaseous drinks shall be avoided. Walking in the cabin during the flights relieves the person.  14.32.2. Gastroenteritis  Gastroenteritis is a common intestinal infection that causes vomiting and diarrhea. This is caused by bacteria, viruses or other organisms. Most attacks spontaneously resolve within a few days. If diarrhea and vomiting are severe, they may cause dehydration; this means that there is not enough water in your body.  Symptoms : The most common symptoms of gastroenteritis are diarrhea and vomiting. Many people have stomach pains, fever (high fever) and headache. The symptoms usually last for several days, but may last up to a week.  The symptoms of dehydration   include collapsed eyes, dry mouth and rusting of the tongue, and a small amount of dark and heavily scented urine. Taking plenty of fluids can reduce symptoms.  Protection:   The best way to prevent gastroenteritis is to follow hygiene rules. Wash hands after toilet, before touching food, after working in the garden and playing with pets. Do not use shared towels with people with gastroenteritis and clean the toilets they use regularly.  14.32.3. Appendicitis  Appendicitis is located in the lower right quarter of the abdomen. It develops with a severe pain in the lower right quarter of the abdomen. The pain may hit groins and the patient may get into shock because of the pain. In that case; Keep the patient in her/his most comfortable position. Bending her/his legs towards the abdomen at the sitting position may reduce the pain. Supply the patient with oxygen where required. Put the patient in the recovery position if pain shock and loss of consciousness develops.  14.32.4. Kidney Diseases  Kidneys are located in the lumbar region, in front of the back muscle wall and on the right and left side of the spine symmetrically. Blood flow rate is highly rapid. 20% of the stroke volume per minute passes through kidneys. Pains especially caused by kidney stones are too severe. It is considered as the most severe pain for men and the second most severe pain after normal delivery for women. Keep the patient in her/his most comfortable position, Supply the patient with oxygen if required, Put the patient in the recovery position if pain shock and loss of consciousness develops.  14.33. Pain and Its Types  Pain is continuous and disturbing (differently from the sharp, spontaneous, or dispersed pain). Headache is a pain emerging inside the head, above the eyes, or in skull base. Generally, there are 3 types of pain: Somatic, visceral, and neuropathic. In all these three types, the pain may be chronic or acute.  Somatic pain:   It arises from the activation of pain receptors on the body surface or in the musculoskeletal tissue. The common reason of the somatic pains is the pain felt at the incision place after the operations. In general, the pain increases with activity and decreases with rest.  Visceral pain:   It is the most common pain we feel when our internal organs are damaged or injured. The visceral pain arises from the problems related to the internal organs such as stomach, kidney, gallbladder, urinary bladder, and intestines.  Neuropathic pain:   It arises from damage to or malfunction of the spinal cord and peripheral nerves. It causes the feeling of burning, tingling, drawing, stinging.  14.34. Deep Venous Thrombosis (Economy Class Syndrome)  During or within the first 48 hours after the long-haul flights like the intercontinental air travel, blood accumulation occurs in some of the leg veins especially, as it is not possible to maintain a proper blood circulation due to long-lasting immobility throughout the flight. Long- lasting blood accumulation may result in clots in such places. This situation is observed in the passengers making a long travel by train, car, coach, and airplanes and called   “travel thrombosis” (clotting)   or   economy class syndrome . This situation may also affect the flight and cabin crews as well as the passengers. That the legs remain contracted and motionless in a certain position for hours during the long aircraft travels slows down the blood circulation; that particularly the popliteal veins are squeezed by the edge of the seat blocks the flow of blood in the vein. The compression occurring there causes increase of the intravenous pressure and minimal injury to the veins, slowdown of the blood flow, thickening of the blood, and clotting. This, in turn, causes cramps, pain in the leg, aneurysm, and sensitivity in the leg. These symptoms may appear within the first 24 hours after landing, during the flight, on the first day after the flight, or within the first 15 days after the flight. On average, the time for appearance of the DVT findings has been reported as the fourth day after the travel. Generally, it is observed more frequently in men than women. For deep veins, it means embolism together with coagulation. It is most frequently observed in leg veins.  Reason of Deep Venous Thrombosis  1. Slowdown of the blood flow in the veins (immobility), 2. Damage to vein wall, 3. These are the situations causing faster than normal coagulation of blood. Besides; Since the   pitch is narrow   in the economy class of passenger aircraft, there is no way to extend one's legs sufficiently; and it is very difficult for the window side passengers to get out to the aisle. It is considered that the   DVT risk is higher for the economy class passengers   sitting or sleeping in the same position with knees bent for hours without getting out of their seats.  The DVT risk is also high for the pilots   working in sitting position in the cockpit for hours. Since the cabin crew members are on the move continuously, their DVT risk is very low. The alcoholic drinks consumed during flights cause drainage of more body fluids (through urination), and thus thickening of blood.  Measures against DVT in Long-Haul Flights  Wear roomy and comfortable garments, underwear, socks, and shoes; avoid tight garments blocking your blood circulation. Do not put bags under your feet so as not to prevent leg movements. Avoid using drugs and alcohol unnecessarily for sedation (deep sleep provided by such drugs leads to immobility). If you have any cardiovascular diseases, cancer, or any disease-causing coagulation, you shall absolutely consult with a physician before the flight.  14.35. Circadian Rhythm (24-Hour Rhythm) and Biological Clock  The system that adjusts the timing of numerous functions in our body is called the “ Biological Clock ”. It ensures the operation of several functions bound to certain rhythms (sleeping-wakefulness, menstruation, body heat, etc.). The human body functions to a certain biological rhythm. Some of them have a 24-hour period, and are called   circadian rhythms . The circadian rhythm arranges the temporal relation of each physiological function with the other one. Several functions vary by sleeping or wakefulness. The circadian rhythm is the sleeping/wakefulness rhythm. This rhythm is related to the changes in the body heat.  14.36. Jetlag  Since long distances are covered in short time and different time zones are arrived, deviations occur in biological rhythm, and this synchronization disorder leads to   Jetlag . Since the first day at the destination point lasts shorter than 24 hours as the time zones increase during the eastward flights, the body has difficulty in making up the time lag. Shortening of one-day physiological rhythm leads to a more severe Jetlag.  Effects of jetlag on the body:  Fatigue, sleeplessness, general pain in the body, Sweating, Indigestion, constipation, lack of appetite, Blurred vision, wooziness, Distorted perceptions of time and distance, Delayed reaction, Loss of memory and judgment  Jetlag Management  Two methods can be used in jetlag management: Method 1: Keeping awake until two hours after the flight, then, sleeping/resting for 4 hours; and sleeping for 8 hours before reporting for the next duty. Method 2: It is applied if the stay-over period is less than 24 hours. In that case, follow the time zone clues in the place you have arrived. Besides, he shall have been completed the following trainings successfully: It is indispensable to drink plenty of water to deal with all negative effects of low humidity rate and thirst in the airplane. Avoid alcoholic and caffeinated drinks, and eat light meals. 14.37. Fatigue  Persons do not feel the start of fatigue. Due to slow start, performance decrease may be overlooked; the individual losses his self- criticism ability, and becomes more prone to take bad decisions and fly erroneously. As the fatigue increases, the decision-making skills is lost along with a decrease in all thinking processes. The reaction time is extended. Therefore, fatigue in aviation is a serious safety problem.  Causes of Flight Crews' Fatigue  The flight crews' fatigue depends normally on the following: Circadian rhythm disorder – jetlag, Short-haul flight programs – multi-leg flight days, Bad flight programs – long standby periods, long duty periods, Sleeplessness due to family and private reasons. Although other factors may also their own influences, these are the main reasons.  Symptoms of Flight Crew Fatigue  Several symptoms of the fatigue: Slow reaction time (both physical and cognitive) Errors becoming ordinary Loss of self-criticism ability Brief loss of memory Decreased communication skill and increased communication problems due to anxiety and being on an emotional rollercoaster Reasoning disorder that leads to bad decisions Attention deficit Apathy, negligence  Fatigue Management  Appropriate nutrition and exercises together with a good rest and sleep prevent brief fatigue. Coffee, concentration or willpower does not eliminate fatigue. They may delay its start, but when their effects are over, fatigue becomes severer. If sufficient recovery time cannot be created between short fatigue fits, chronic fatigue may emerge. The only therapy is a long resting period. The detailed information on what the Cabin Crew Members shall do when they feel fatigued is available in Section 6.1.1.1. Deterioration of Medical Fitness and the Section 6.1.2.15. Fatigue.  14.38. Sleep and Sleep Credit/Debit  During a sleep, the body does not only relieve physical tiredness of the day but also carries out the basic organization of the cognitive processes. The sleep debit can be calculated easily by using a simple system in which each slept hour is given +2 points and each awake hour is given -1 point. Assume that an individual normally sleeps for 8 hours. When s/he wakes up, s/he has accumulated +16 points. When the same individual keeps awake for 16 hours, s/he loses 16 points; and thus, s/he finishes the day with zero point. In the forthcoming days, the same process continues, and the individual's score never goes down below zero. The person who has less sleep points is more prone to sleeping. Normally, when his/her sleep credit is low or zero, the individual sleeps. The gradual decrease in the sleep credit may accumulate to become minus in time, and create "cumulative sleep debit". important to realize the low performance that emerges with this sleep deprivation and increases with the altitude. The sleep debit and fatigue may lead to microsleep. Microsleeps are spontaneous and uncontrollable sleep periods that lasts for seconds and sometimes minutes. The only cure of the sleep debit is sleep.  Quality Sleep  People need different amounts of sleep. Some hints for a quality sleep are as follows: Avoid physical and mental works and exercises before the sleep time. Get rest for at least 30 minutes before going to bed. Do not go to bed unless you feel sleepy. A light reading or music may relax the mind. You may have a warm shower before going to bed (it relaxes the muscles and body). Ventilate the room, and preserve the room temperature (it shall be neither too cold nor too hot). Avoid smoking, alcohol and caffeine. Drink a warm milky drink (neither coffee nor tea). Do not go to bed either hungry or full (eat your last meal 3 hours before going to bed). Melatonin  It is a hormone released by the body and arranging the biological rhythm of the body. The hormone is sensitive to light and electromagnetic waves. Sleeplessness does not affect the melatonin production, but the light suppresses the hormone emission. Melatonin is the growth hormone for children, and plays a significant role in cancer protection.  14.39. Pressure-Related Diseases  Barotrauma  Barotrauma, as the name suggests, is a condition that occurs when pressure changes in the external environment are not balanced by the middle ear and sinuses. When traveling by aircraft, it can be felt especially during take-off and landing. Due to the structure of the ear, it is more likely to be felt in the moments of landing. If the pressure equalization in the middle ear is disturbed by trauma, this can lead to perforation of the eardrum.  What does cause Barotrauma on board Aircraft?  At the moment of landing, the eardrum stretches inward due to pressure changes, causing pain that radiates from the ear to the head. While the pressure change can be equalized by releasing air from the ear during take-off, air shall be pumped into the ear during landing.  14.39.1. Eustachian Tube and Barotrauma  Function of the Eustachian Tube:  The eustachian tube is a channel that provides passage between the region behind it and called nasopharynx and the middle ear. This channel enables to middle ear to take air, and also create a road so that the secretions in this region can flow into the nasopharynx. It enables the middle ear to adapt to the pressure changes in the external environment. Gas expansion in the middle ear during ascent causes the eardrum to bulge outward. Eustachian tube passively opens and transmits air to the nasopharynx. Pressure rises during descent and, decreasing the gas volume in the middle ear space, creates a negative pressure. This blocks the passive passage of air from the nasopharynx to the middle ear. Nasopharynx shall actively supply the middle ear with air to equalize this.  Barotrauma:  The sickness caused by the pressure difference between the body cavities containing air and the surrounding atmosphere. If the Eustachian tube remains closed, the pressure on two sides of the ear drum will be unequal. This is called barotrauma or barotitis media. Ear Barotrauma is one of the ear-nose-throat problems frequently encountered in aviation.  Situations with Barotrauma Risk:  Upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) Allergies and rhinitis (flu) Sinusitis Nasal problems (stuffiness, turbinate hypertrophy, etc.) Ear infections Throat infections External auditory canal congestion (earplugs, earwax) In case of existence of the abovementioned disorders, the eustachian tube entrance may be clogged. This prevents the equalization of pressure.  Symptoms of Ear Barotrauma:  The main symptoms, especially during the descent, are intense earache and partial hearing loss. In addition to these, fullness, humming noise, nausea and dizziness may also be observed. In light cases, fullness is felt without ache. If it recurs frequently, middle ear calcification may happen. Its severe cases may lead to hymen rupture. If you have such complaints during the descent, please apply to the physician's office immediately after landing.  First Aid Treatment for Barotrauma:  The best protection is to know barotrauma, and to make the pressure equalization on time and correctly. During descent especially: Yawning Swallowing (you can drink water) Chewing (chewing gum, etc.) If they do not help, and if there is no active infection, pressure equalization maneuvers shall be done:  Valsalva Maneuver:   Sending air to ears after closing mouth and nose opens the eustachian tube, and allows the air flowing into and out of the middle ear by equalizing the air pressure at both sides of the eardrum.  Toynbee Maneuver:   Swallowing by closing the mouth and nose may also help. In the event that the infants have earache, it is recommended that the infant sucks a pacifier or feeding bottle, or is breastfed by its mother. Allowing the infant to cry will also relieve the pressure in the infant's ears. If you have URTI (Upper Respiratory Tract Infection), influenza, nose stuffiness before the flight duty, you shall be examined by the physician. 14.40. Airsickness (Motion Sickness)  While our brains perceive the body position and the motion; The inner ear analyzes the motion data such as revolving, moving back and forth and up and down, The eyes analyze the position (upside-down, on the right side, etc.) of the body in its surroundings as well as the data they acquire by observing the direction of the movement, and The sensory receptors in the feet, hip, skin, muscles and joints analyze the data which inform which part of the body is below and touches the ground. The motion sickness emerges as a result of the dissonance arising when the eyes, inner ear and the sensory systems cannot adapt to a motor stimulant. The frequency of the motion sickness varies by the individual's sensitivity and the strength of the stimulant.  Risk Factors:  Gender: Women are more susceptible to motion sickness than men. Age: The frequency of the sickness is at the top level at the age of 12, and decreases gradually as the age increases. Hormonal factors: Pregnancy, menstrual period and contraceptive pills increase the susceptibility. In the event of another disease that affects the balance system in the inner ear and the visual system, the susceptibility increases. Those who have migraine are more susceptible to motion sickness.  Symptoms:  Nausea Vomiting Cold sweat Paleness Headache Feeling sluggish Sleepiness Dizziness Depression Such symptoms generally disappear when the motion ends.  If you are Susceptible to Motion Sickness,  Drink sufficient water before and during the flight, and avoid water loss. Eat less and spiceless foods. Wear large, comfortable and cool garments. Concentrate on an activity, and keep your brain active (but, avoid reading anything because it would worsen the symptoms). When you sit down on your seat, take the airsickness bag and keep it readily available. If you have frequently recurring symptoms, apply to our medical examiner offices. It is asserted that consuming caffeine increases the effectiveness of the drugs curing the motion sickness. There are studies suggesting that ginger may also be used to sure the motion sickness. 14.41. Stress-Induced Diseases  It is an individual's reaction to stressor stimulants that disturb his/her stability and adaptation, even cause diseases.  Stress Factors:   Stress factors are defined in 3 categories as physical, physiological and emotional.  Effects of Stress  1.   Physical effects:   Pupil dilation, fast breathing, increased heart rate, redness, perspiration, etc. 2.   Emotional effects:   Anxiety, depression, fast crying, rapidly and continuously changing state of mind, decreased self-reliance, excessive sensitivity, etc. 3.   Cognitive Effects:   Lack of concentration, difficulty in decision-making, forgetfulness, wooziness, etc. 4.   Behavioral Effects:   Excessive consumption of tobacco, alcohol and the other substances. 5.   Health Effects:   Headache, sleep disorder, back and muscle pains, high tension, heart attack.  Chronic stress threatens the individual's health in the long term. Stress Management  Stress management is an individual's behavior of dealing with stress. In order to perform stress management, first of all, the individual shall acknowledge that the stress causes a problem.  Ways to deal with Stress  In order to deal with stress, the individual shall first acknowledge that s/he is under stress, and want to do something to do about that. The better your physical and emotional health is, the less stress affects you. To achieve that, the general recommendations are as follows: 1.   Eating Well : An appropriate diet providing sufficient amount of energy from four basic groups of food provides you with all foods you need to deal with stress and appear healthy. 2.   Doing Exercises Regularly:   Regular exercise increases your heart's strength, breathing capacity, blood influx into muscles, and decreases the stress. 3.   Relaxation:   Effective relaxation decreases your heart and breathing rates, increases your musculoskeletal strength, and organizes the cognitive functions. 4.   Entertainment:   Spare time for some entertainment on daily basis. 5.   Changing Tactics:   Restart the problem-solving process. When you find a new approach, try it. 6.   Progress slowly :   You cannot decrease all stressors in your live at once. Therefore, focus on one or two stressors in the beginning.  If you cannot cope with stress on your own, receive professional help absolutely.  14.41.1. Panic Attack  A panic attack is a sudden onset of intense boredom or fear, which occasionally recurs, leaving people in horror. The Panic Attack starts abruptly, intensifies and becomes more intense within 10 minutes; usually after continuing 10-30 minutes (infrequently up to 1 hour) it ends automatically.  Panic attack indications and symptoms:   Panic attack indications and symptoms include palpitations, chest pain or discomfort, shortness of breath or rapid breathing, overwhelming, shivering or shaking, choking sensation, sweating, nausea, dizziness, or feeling like you might faint, numbness or tingling sensation, chills, horripilation or hot flushes, fear of death, losing control or feeling of going mad.  14.42. Techniques for Transportation of Ill/Injured Persons 14.42.1. General Rules for Transportation of Ill/Injured Persons  Do not risk your own health while carrying the ill/injured person. Observe the rules stated below in order to avoid strain and injury: Pay attention to being close to the ill/injured person while starting to apply transportation methods. Use longer and stronger muscle groups. Bend the ill/injured person's knees and hips in order to maintain the tension of her/his back (it reduces the risk of spine injuries). Place one of the ill/injured person's leg a little bit forward and make sure that s/he supports her/his feet on the ground. Emergency Transportation Techniques 14.42.2.1. Dragging Techniques  Dragging ill/injured persons is a considerably helpful technique. If especially overweight and heavily-built persons are required to be dragged, this technique may be preferred in order to prevent any injuries in cases where such people shall be discharged from any place too narrow and low to pass through. Take the physical capacity of the first aider into consideration. Make use of blankets if possible. Dragging techniques are as follows: Dragging by ankles, Dragging by armpits.  14.42.2.2. Transportation Technique for Injured Persons Stuck in Vehicles (RENTEK Maneuver)  It is used to discharge injured accident survivors without damaging the spinal cord in cases where special attention is needed to eliminate any risks. This technique is applied in such dangerous cases as respiratory arrest, fire threat or explosion. First of all; Assess the accident site. Ensure the peripheral security when it is estimated that there is any explosion or fire threat. Check his/her conscious by tapping the patient’s/injured person’s shoulders lightly and saying, “Are you OK?”. Observe the injured person's respiration (by paying attention to her/his chest heaving). If respiration is observed, and there is no risk for fire/explosion in the vehicle; Do not take the injured person out. Secure her/his neck with any available items. If no respiration is observed, and there is a risk for fire/explosion in the vehicle; Make sure that the injured person's feet are not stuck between the pedals, and release the safety belt. Move to the injured person's side. Secure the injured person's neck by holding her/his arm with one hand and her/his jaw with the other (gently). Emergency Childbirth  Any vaginal bleeding that occurs in pregnancy shall be considered as a threat of miscarriage or premature birth depending on the week of pregnancy. In the face of such a situation, the pregnant passenger shall not be made walk but instead laid down on her left side. The Commander shall be informed of the situation immediately. Besides, along with the progress of pregnancy, the rib cage expands, and the diaphragm rises by 4 cm. The lung capacity decreases. Besides that, the oxygen consumption increases. Therefore, every time the pregnant passenger suffers from respiratory distress, she shall be given oxygen immediately. When it becomes evident that any passenger will give birth, this occurrence is under the responsibility of cabin crew members if medical assistance cannot be provided. The Cabin Chief or any Cabin Crew Member assigned by the Cabin Chief shall undertake this responsibility, form a team and give commands. The first thing to do is to collect first aid supplies like tablecloths, napkins, paper towels, blankets, pillows, pillow cases, sanitary napkins, clean nylon bags, air sick bags, first aid kit, and Emergency Medical Kit that you can make use of in the course of childbirth. Find an appropriate place to assist the childbirth. The optimal place is the front row seats of economy class or any available part of the galley. In order to make the floor waterproof, place nylon bags on the seats and floor; then lay paper towels or newspapers over the bags and finally cover all of them with blanket. Rinse your hands carefully and fill one of the air sickness bags with soap water and the other with water so that you can clean your hands in the course of childbirth if required. Get the pregnant passenger urinate beforehand to protect her urinary bladder against damage in the course of childbirth. At the moment of childbirth, lay the pregnant passenger down on supine position and ensure that her knees are bended upwards towards her stomach. Make sure that the pregnant passenger lies down on her left arm all the time except for the moment of childbirth. Take all clothes that will prevent the course of childbirth.  14.43.1. Stages of Childbirth  Childbirth occurs in stages happening in a given order. First of all, the mouth of the womb becomes ready to open and get thinner. The plug closing this region may be thrown. This is called sign. The pregnant passenger may specify it as bleeding. If she informs something like that to the cabin crew, the cabin crew shall consider that the delivery has begun and give information to the cockpit immediately. Childbirth occurs in three stages;  First Stage:   Opening of the womb mouth sufficiently to let the baby's head to pass following the beginning of contractions. This period lasts 12-14 hours for those who give birth to their first children, and 6-8 hours for those giving birth to their second or later children. Prolongation of this period is directly proportional to sitting the mother down and not letting her to move. In this period, the mother shall not be given solid foods. In the beginning, the contractions are mild and irregular. Then, the contraction happens every 2-3 minutes, and lasts for 60 to 90 seconds. In this period, the mother may be nauseous and vomit. The mother shall be laid continuously on her left side.  Second Stage:   The period between dilation of the cervix and the birth of the infant. At this stage, the mother feels an intensive need to strain, and a pressure occurs on the anus. The mother may say she needs to go to the toilet; she shall never be raised. Her intestines may be purged unintentionally; urinary leakage may be observed. This stage may last 30 minutes to 2 hours. In this period, the duty of the cabin crew is to support the mother to strain herself. It is important that the strain is simultaneous with the contractions. When the contractions are over, the mother is said to breathe easily, and she may also be given oxygen.  Pushing Technique  If the mother strains in compliance with the relevant technique, this will shorten the second stage. Otherwise, straining will only tire the mother out. The mother shall take a deep breath when the contractions are most severe, and strain strongly without exhaling and by keeping her mouth closed. While straining the hip and the waist shall be in the C position, rest her chin on her chest, strain with all her strength towards her rectum, and push the baby. Do not intervene with the childbirth under any circumstances until the baby's head is delivered fully at the moment of delivery. Do not make the mother strain as of the moment when the baby's head is out. Tell the mother to inhale deeply. In order to prevent straining, the mouth is opened, and short but strong breaths are taken. After the baby's head is out, do not touch its head. Wipe the baby's mouth and nose with a clean and dry cloth. When the baby's head is out, it is faced downwards. Therefore, in order that its shoulders can move out, the baby will turn its head towards the right or left leg. After this turning movement, first the upper shoulder and then the lower shoulder of the baby will move out. It is necessary to be careful in this period. Third Stage:   This is the period between childbirth and the expulsion of placenta. Never take the mother's part of the umbilical cord, or force her to eject the placenta. It may take 30-45 minutes for the placenta to be ejected. In this period, mild contractions may be observed in the mother. The massage to be applied by a Cabin Crew Member to the stiffness (which is the womb) of grapefruit size by using her ten fingers will shorten this period. When the placenta is ejected, put it into a clean nylon bag. When the placenta is ejected, the delivery is completed.  Assistance to Mother  The first hours after the delivery are very important for the mother and the baby. Check the mother's blood pressure, body heat, breathing rate and pulse rate frequently. The mother may be observed to be weak, tired, cold and bleeding. Apply the appropriate first aid to them. Continuous bleeding, clot ejection, or turning of the blood color into light and bright red within the first 20-30 minutes after the delivery indicate abnormal bleeding. If the mother breastfeeds her baby, this will help the womb to get over and the bleeding to decrease.  CAUTION:   Do not administer Metergin, which induces uterine contractions, to hypertension patients (140 mm/Hg and over). If the mother experiences a uterine rupture during the delivery, place a sterile gauze on the ruptured area and then apply cold compress with an ice bag (if available). Keep the mother in a lying position until medical assistance arrives at the arrival station. You can provide the mother with liquid foods if required; but do not give any solid food under any circumstances.  14.44. Death Onboard  If you suspect that a passenger has died, inform the flight crew immediately. Only physicians can decide whether the person has died or not. Do not move the passenger and secure her/him with the seat belts. Ensure that as few passengers as possible are informed and keep the situation under control. Treat the passengers who are traveling with the deceased passenger thoughtfully and kindly. Try to calm them down. The procedures to be followed are as described in   EK.10.73.001 Operation Manual Part-A, Section 8.3. Flight Procedures.  14.45. AED (Automatic External Defibrillator [Electroshock] Device)  The principles for the use of defibrillator and its delivery after its use are detailed in   EK.10.71.003 Cabin Crew Aircraft Types Manual , Chapter 6.0. Emergency Equipment.  Who can use This Device on board Aircraft:  a) The person shall be a physician/have received AED training, b) The Cabin Crew Members who have received training and certification for Basic Life Support (BLS) and AED.  Contents of Defibrillator:  Defibrillator is available in a protective bag. Besides, there is a Ready Kit tied to the handle of the defibrillator. === Sayfa 298 ===
What are the general principles of AED usage?  AED does not assess respiration of the ill/injured person. Before treating the ill/injured person, it is necessary to evaluate absolutely whether the scene of incident is risky for the first-aider, the ill/injured person, and the people around. The regions to which the pads are to be affixed shall be dry. If the ill/injured person’s chest is wet, the chest shall be dried before placing the pads. The chest hair or jewelry, accessory, etc. around the neck and/or on the chest creates problem in transmission of the pads. In such cases, the materials available in the ready kit next to the device, such as scissors, gloves, razor, etc. can be used. The jewelries, etc. shall be stored in a separate bag. If there is any open wound in the region where the pads are to be affixed, the pads shall not be affixed on the wound. Besides, if there are medication patches affixed to the chest, first these patches shall be removed, and then the pads shall be affixed.  In which cases shall AED not be used?  AED shall not be applied to the ill/injured person under rain, on wet and metal surface. In such a case, the ill/injured person is pulled onto a dry surface, their rib cage is dried, and AED shall be used only if it can be ensured that the pads and the rib cage can be prevented from getting wet again. It shall not be used in the environments where there are flammable gases and dense oxygen due to fire and explosion hazard. Additionally, while treating a patient given oxygen continuously, first the oxygen source shall be disconnected and moved away.  15. Cargo Operation onboard Passenger Aircraft  Cargo is not carried in the cabin of passenger aircraft in the fleet. With commercial passenger aircraft, cargo is carried only in the cargo hold of the aircraft. In case of fire in the cabin, the protective mask, if any, must be taken off before wearing the smoke hood in order that the smoke hood fits the face fully. In case of emergency, before the cabin crew gives the relevant command and the oxygen mask is put on, the protective mask, if any, must be taken off. Reporting: The cabin crews report the unsafe situations they have detected during the cargo operation over the AQD Portal or mobile application by selecting one of the Cabin Safety e-Report (CSR) or Hazard e-Report (HAZ) headings.  15.1. Cargo Operation in which Cargo is carried in Cargo Compartment only and Cargo or Passengers are not carried in Cabin (All Aircraft Types)  To the cargo operations in which the cargo is carried in the cargo compartment only, and no cargo or passenger is carried in the cabin of passenger aircraft, the cabin crew members in the number specified in   PR.73.016 Procedure for Cabin Safety in Flights performed with Reduced or No Cabin Crew are assigned (if 2 persons are assigned, the duties are distributed by the Cabin Chief [as equally as possible]). To the flights with resting, a cabin crew composed of minimum two members at least one of whom is Cabin Chief is assigned. In the relevant operation, the cabin crew(s) perform their duties by applying the following differences, in line with the principles specified in EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual. The cabin chief distributes the duties and responsibilities specified in the Cabin Crew Checklist.  Fire Procedure:  a. Cabin crew composed of 1 person: The flight crew is informed of the fire immediately by the nearest interphone; the necessary equipment/spare equipment is obtained; and the fire is responded (if there is non-revenue passenger on board the aircraft [see 15.1.1. Carriage of Non-Revenue Passenger on Flights during which Cargo is not carried in Aircraft Cabin (All Aircraft Types)], the passengers are guided as much as possible). b. Cabin crew composed of 2 persons: The first Cabin Crew Member who saw the fire is responsible for informing the second Cabin Crew Member of the situation and extinguishing the fire. The second Cabin Crew Member gives information to the flight crew at every stage of the fire and brings the spare equipment (and guides the passengers if there is non-revenue passenger on board the aircraft as specified in the Section 15.1.1. Carriage of Non-Revenue Passenger on Flights during which Cargo is not carried in Aircraft Cabin (All Aircraft Types)). a. Cabin crew composed of 1 person: The principles under EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual, Section 8.2.3. Procedures for Opening/Closing the Door, Door Slide Positions apply. Differently, when a cabin crew composed of 1 person is responsible for two doors, s/he performs everything s/he must perform at all doors. If it becomes necessary to open a door in non-routine cases, it is possible to disarm only the door that must be opened instead of all doors, depending on the approval of the commander. b. Cabin crew composed of 2 persons: The principles under EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual, Section 8.2.3. Procedures for Opening/Closing the Door, Door Slide Positions apply. Differently, the slides of the left side doors are ARMED/DISARMED by CC and the slides of the right-side doors by CA1. While carrying out the application, the principles that must be followed when two cabin crew members are responsible for opposite doors are followed. If it becomes necessary to open a door in non-routine cases, it is possible to disarm only the door that must be opened instead of all doors, depending on the approval of the commander.  Evacuation : During a potential evacuation, the primary exits are the doors in the cabin crew station zone, which are used in taxi, takeoff and landing (TTL) (During ditching, the 3L/R doors of B777 aircraft and the aft doors of B737 aircraft are out of this scope. B777 3L/R doors are used as secondary exit in case of ditching, and slide has to be disarmed if it is necessary to open. The aft doors of B737 are not used in ditching. The escape slides on the A321 emergency exit doors (2L/R and 3L/R) do not detach from the aircraft and are not used for ditching. Therefore, these doors are DISARMED and opened. The cabin crew stations to sit during TTL and cruise are specified in Table-29 Cabin Crew Stations during TTL and Cruise in the section 15.1. Cargo Operation in which Cargo is carried in Cargo Compartment only and Cargo or Passengers are not carried in Cabin (All Aircraft Types). During an evacuation, after making sure that no one is left, the aircraft is left by taking the materials to be taken in case of evacuation according to the section of the relevant aircraft type in   EK.10.71.003 Cabin Crew Aircraft Types Manual.  Incapacitated Pilot:  The incapacitated pilot application is carried out as per the principles in EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual, Section 8.3.6. Incapacitated Pilot and   Quick Reference Handlist (QRH), section 1.26. Incapacitated Pilot. During a flight performed with a cabin crew composed of 2 persons, if the duty that requires one person to be present in the cockpit and read the checklist is performed by the Cabin Chief, the second Cabin Crew Member does not leave the door 1L unattended.  Decompression:  The Decompression application is carried out as per the principles in EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual, Section 8.3.2.2.   Cabin Decompression.  Monitoring of Cabin:  The cabin and lavatories are observed by walking along the cabin aisle at regular intervals not longer than 30 minutes during the flight. On the flights performed with a cabin crew of two, the cabin crew members do not come together in the galleys when they are not in the cabin for monitoring purpose. Pre-Flight Passenger Briefing is read and also the relevant demo is performed by using the demo kit. Number and Composition of Cabin Crew. Since the number of cabin crew members will be the same with the one on revenue passenger transportation flights, and there will be no cargo in the cabin, the revenue passenger transportation principles in EK.10.71.001 Cabin Crew Manual apply.
